9.title: The Source of Love: We Love Because God First Loved Us

mem.t: We love him, because he first loved us.

s: Find somewhere near water for a walk: a riverside, a lake, the beach, or a fountain in the park. Talk as you walk about what moved you this week.
Each share one specific moment when you knew God loved you. It could be the day you were saved, or something small that happened recently.
Take turns finishing this sentence: “Because God loved me first, this week I want to be the first to do this for you: …”
Slowly read 1 John 4:19 together, then hold hands and pray: “Lord, be the spring of love in our home.”

lessons.title: Broken Cisterns
lessons.theme: Human love runs dry because we have left the spring of living water

v: “For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters, and cut out cisterns for themselves: broken cisterns that can’t hold water.
Jesus answered her, “Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again,
but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again; but the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life.”

lessons.still: Be still and honestly ask yourself: “Lately, how much love is left in my heart?” You don’t need to pretend you’re full. Tell the Lord: “Lord, sometimes I’m dry and tired. Today I want to come back to you, the spring.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Treating my spouse as my spring is a hidden form of the self-ruled life: I want you to satisfy me. When they can’t, I become disappointed and blame them. When we turn our focus back to Jesus and drink deeply from him, we stop demanding from our spouse and instead let living water flow out to them.
lessons.jesus: On the greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink!” (John 7:37). He did not scold people for being thirsty; he simply invited them to come to him. Jesus is our example: he himself often withdrew to be with the Father, and he invites the thirsty to return to the source.
lessons.pray: Spring of living water, we confess that we often leave you and then demand love and approval from each other, and we both end up thirstier. Today we come back to you. Let your love become a spring within us, so that we stop demanding from each other and instead receive from you and let it flow to each other. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: Picture a household water tank that has to supply the whole family every day for showers, cooking, and laundry. If the tank isn’t connected to the mains and has only the water first poured into it, then however carefully you use it, one day it will run dry. Many marriages grow weary not because one person is especially bad, but because both are supplying each other from their own limited tank, and it keeps getting lower.

Through Jeremiah, God said his people had committed two evils: “they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters, and cut out cisterns for themselves: broken cisterns that can’t hold water” (Jeremiah 2:13). In ancient Israel, living water was flowing spring water, while a cistern was a pit cut into the rock to collect rainwater. People set aside a spring that never stops flowing to rely on a pit they had dug themselves, and a leaky one at that.

In marriage we often dig cisterns too: we hope our spouse’s praise, thoughtfulness, and romance will fill our hearts. But our spouse is also a person who needs water; they are not the spring. Jesus told the Samaritan woman, “Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again” (John 4:13), and also, “the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life” (John 4:14). The source of love is not in our spouse; it is in Jesus.
q: Lately, in what area do I most often expect my spouse to “fill” me?
When was the last time I was truly filled with love by God? What was that like?
talk: How do you think our “water level” has been lately: full, half full, or nearly empty? Each share why.
What simple habit could help us return together to God, the spring, every day?
acts: Morning and evening today, spend three minutes quietly telling the Lord: “I’m thirsty.”
Write down one need you often demand from your spouse, and hand it to God
Don’t ask to be loved today; be the first to thank your spouse
lessons.noon: “whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again” — Lord Jesus, right now I come to you to drink. Satisfy my heart.

lessons.title: God Is Love
lessons.theme: Love is defined not by feelings but by the cross

v: Beloved, let’s love one another, for love is of God; and everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God.
He who doesn’t love doesn’t know God, for God is love.
By this God’s love was revealed in us, that God has sent his only born Son into the world that we might live through him.
In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.

lessons.still: Quietly read these three words: “God is love.” Let them settle in your heart. Tell the Lord: “Lord, teach me to stop defining love by my own feelings, and to learn what love is from you.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The human view says “love is my feeling,” and the focus is on myself; God’s view says “love is God’s nature,” and the focus is on God. Change your mindset and your life will change: when we learn love from the cross, we stop asking, “Do I still feel it?” and start asking, “How does God want me to love?”
lessons.jesus: In the parable of the prodigal son, Jesus describes how, “while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him” (Luke 15:20). The father did not wait for his son to prove himself first; he ran to him first. Through this picture Jesus tells us that God’s love always moves first.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for sending your Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins, showing us what true love is. Renew our definition of love so that we are no longer led around by our feelings. When we are tired and the feelings fade, remind us of the love of the cross, and let our home be built on your love. Amen.
teach: If you want to teach a child what “red” is, the best way isn’t to write an essay; it’s to point to an apple and say, “Look, that’s red.” The Bible teaches us about love the same way. John does not start with an abstract definition; he points to God and says, “God is love” (1 John 4:8). To know what love is, we look at who God is and what God has done.

John goes on: “In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (1 John 4:10). An “atoning sacrifice” is an offering for sin that turns away God’s righteous anger. In other words, God’s love does not ignore sin; he pays the price himself to deal with it. Love is not an emotional high; it is an action on the cross.

This changes the way we see marriage. The world says: love while the feeling lasts, and split up when it’s gone. The Bible says: “love is of God” (1 John 4:7). Our love for our spouse is not manufactured by romance; it is received from God and then lived out. When the tide of feeling goes out, the love of the cross still stands, and that is the true foundation of marriage.
q: Is my inner definition of love closer to a feeling, or to the action of the cross?
When I think of “God is love,” what past hurt or experience makes it hard for me to believe it?
talk: In our marriage, when have you felt my love not because of romance, but because I paid a price?
If you had to describe love with one everyday action, what would you choose? Why?
acts: Copy out 1 John 4:10 and put it on your phone’s home screen or the fridge
Do one small thing today that costs you something but helps your spouse feel loved
Before bed, say together: “God is love, and our home belongs to him.”
lessons.noon: “God is love” — Father, right now I rest in your love, and I want to carry it to my family.

lessons.title: Filled with Love First
lessons.theme: An empty cup can’t pour; we must be filled with God’s love before we can love our spouse

v: that he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, that you may be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person,
that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, to the end that you, being rooted and grounded in love,
may be strengthened to comprehend with all the saints what is the width and length and height and depth,
and to know Christ’s love which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.
and hope doesn’t disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.

lessons.still: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up, as if holding an empty cup. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, I want to love my family, but I find I’m often empty. Today, by your Spirit, pour your love into my heart.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: When we love our spouse from the head by ourselves, we soon become anxious and worn out; when we live from the heart by the Spirit, love has a source. Life first, then relationship: first let our own lives be filled with God’s love, and our marriage will have strength to be renewed. Change begins with me, and it begins with me returning to God.
lessons.jesus: Before Jesus began his public ministry, at his baptism he heard the Father say, “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Mark 1:11). He had not yet performed a single miracle, yet he was first affirmed by the Father and filled with the Father’s love. Jesus shows us that serving and loving others flow out of our identity as the beloved.
lessons.pray: Lord, we often try to love in our own strength, and the more we love, the more tired we become. By your Spirit, strengthen us with power in our inner being, so that we may grasp how wide and long and high and deep the love of Christ is. Holy Spirit, pour God’s love abundantly into our hearts, and let our home overflow with your love. Amen.
teach: On a plane, the flight attendant always reminds us: “If the oxygen masks drop, put on your own mask before helping the person next to you.” That isn’t selfish; it’s simply true. Without oxygen yourself, you can’t save anyone else. Marriage is the same. We often try to go straight to loving our spouse and forget that we first need to be filled with God’s love.

Paul prayed that God would grant the Ephesian church “that you may be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person” (Ephesians 3:16), so that they “may be strengthened to comprehend with all the saints what is the width and length and height and depth” (Ephesians 3:18) of Christ’s love. This “comprehending” is not just head knowledge; it is lived experience. When we truly experience how wide, long, high, and deep Christ’s love is, our hearts are stretched open.

Romans says, “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us” (Romans 5:5). “Poured” means emptied out in abundance, not handed out drop by drop. God does not ration his love stingily; he pours it out lavishly through the Holy Spirit. What we need to do each day is hold our cup before him: reading Scripture, praying, worshiping, being still. Let him fill us, and let it overflow to our family.
q: Lately, have I been forcing myself to love my family while running on an “empty cup”? What are the signs?
Do I have a time each day when I truly set my heart before God and let him fill it?
talk: When do you feel especially “empty”? How can I come alongside you as you return to God?
Could we work out together which time of day each of us, or both of us together, can draw near to God?
acts: Tomorrow morning, read a passage of Scripture before you pick up your phone
Take one minute today to tell God three ways you have felt his love
Ask your spouse: “What can I pray for you today?”
lessons.noon: “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us” — Holy Spirit, right now pour God’s love into my heart again.

lessons.title: From Demanding Love to Loving First
lessons.theme: Those forgiven much love much; only those who know they are loved can love first

v: Turning to the woman, he said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? I entered into your house, and you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears, and wiped them with the hair of her head.
You gave me no kiss, but she, since the time I came in, has not ceased to kiss my feet.
You didn’t anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment.
Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But one to whom little is forgiven, loves little.”
He said to her, “Your sins are forgiven.”
We love him, because he first loved us.

lessons.still: Recall the moment you first understood that your sins were forgiven. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, you have forgiven me so much. Today I don’t want to just wait for others to be good to me first.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: “You first, then me” is the negotiation of the self-ruled life; “God loved me first, so I’ll love you first” is the self-emptied life. Pride provokes pride and leaves us in a standoff; humility inspires humility, and the one who takes the first step often opens the door for both.
lessons.jesus: In everyone’s eyes Zacchaeus was a sinner, yet before he had repented, Jesus looked up and said, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house” (Luke 19:5). Jesus accepted him first and entered his house first, and only then was Zacchaeus’ life turned around. Jesus is our example of loving first.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for loving us first, while we were still sinners. We confess that we often wait for the other to change first, and we end up at a standstill. Help us know more deeply how greatly we have been forgiven, so that our love may grow too, and make us willing to take the first step: to be gentle first, to apologize first, to embrace first. Amen.
teach: Imagine two people at a door, each waiting for the other to open it. One says, “Apologize first, and I’ll forgive you.” The other says, “Be gentle first, and I won’t be harsh.” Both have a point, yet both are still standing outside. Many couples get stuck exactly like this, not because they don’t want love, but because each is waiting for the other to give first.

Simon the Pharisee invited Jesus to dinner but gave him no water for his feet, while a sinful woman wet Jesus’ feet with her tears. Jesus said, “her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But one to whom little is forgiven, loves little” (Luke 7:47). Her love was not a way to earn forgiveness. She knew she had been forgiven much, and love naturally poured out of her.

John puts it simply: “We love him, because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). God is always the one who moves first. The more I understand how much I owed God and how much grace I have received, the less I will keep score with my spouse about who goes first. Moving from “you have to love me first” to “I’m willing to love you first” is not losing out; it is the natural response of someone who is loved.
q: In what matter have I been waiting for my spouse to change first, apologize first, or give first?
Do I feel I have been “forgiven little,” and so my love for my spouse is little too?
talk: Is there something where you’d like us to stop waiting on each other and both take the first step together?
If I were to do one thing first today to show my love, what would you most like it to be? If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down one thing you want to do for them first.
acts: In one small matter today, don’t wait for your spouse; go first
Tell your spouse: “Thank you. I want to do this for you first.”
Write down three things God has forgiven you for, and thank him
lessons.noon: “We love him, because he first loved us” — Lord, you loved me first; right now I choose to love first.

lessons.title: Remaining in Love
lessons.theme: When we remain in the Lord’s love, love is no longer forced but flows from life

v: Even as the Father has loved me, I also have loved you. Remain in my love.
If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love, even as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love.
I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.
“This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you.
We know and have believed the love which God has for us. God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him.
In this, love has been made perfect among us, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment, because as he is, even so we are in this world.
There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment. He who fears is not made perfect in love.

lessons.still: Look back over this week: broken cisterns, God is love, being filled with love, loving first. Be still for a moment and tell the Lord: “Lord, I don’t want to just visit you now and then. I want to live in your love.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Fear often makes us cling tightly to control, which is one face of the self-ruled life. Remaining in God’s love means letting Jesus reign; instead of trading control for security, we find our security in his love. The self-emptied are not afraid of losing themselves, so they are free to love.
lessons.jesus: However busy Jesus was, he often returned to the Father: “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there” (Mark 1:35). His whole life was lived in the Father’s love, which is why he could keep on loving in the face of crowds, misunderstanding, and the cross.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for loving us just as the Father has loved you. Help us remain in your love, no longer bound by fear and no longer protecting ourselves through control. Let your perfect love drive out the fear in our hearts, and make our home a place where your love lives. Amen.
teach: Picture a grape branch. It never grits its teeth trying to produce fruit; it needs only one thing: to stay attached to the vine. Sap flows into the branch naturally, and fruit grows naturally. Jesus said, “Even as the Father has loved me, I also have loved you. Remain in my love” (John 15:9). To “remain” means to settle in and not leave. Love in marriage is like this too: it isn’t sustained by one big sprint, but by a lasting connection.

John says, “he who remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him” (1 John 4:16). Then he adds, “There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). Behind many marital conflicts is actually fear: fear of being looked down on, fear of being abandoned, fear of not being good enough. As we remain in God’s perfect love, these fears gradually lose their power to control us.

This week we have seen that human love runs dry and God alone is the source; that love is defined by the cross; and that we must first be filled before we can love first. Finally, Jesus ties it all together: “love one another, even as I have loved you” (John 15:12). This is not a heavy command; it is what a person who lives in love naturally looks like. Our home can become a place where God’s love settles and lives.
q: In my relationship with my spouse, what fear most often drives my reactions?
Which verse touched me most this week? How do I want to let it live in my heart?
talk: This week, when did you feel more of my love? What did you feel in your heart then?
Could we make a small agreement for our home to “remain in the Lord’s love”? For example, praying together for one minute every night.
acts: Name one fear you have in your marriage, and entrust it to God
Make a small agreement with your spouse to draw near to God together every day
Memorize 1 John 4:19, and say it aloud at least three times today
lessons.noon: “perfect love casts out fear” — Lord, right now I hand my fear to you and rest in your perfect love.

mem.t: Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud,

s: Before you head out, each secretly prepare a small surprise that costs little but that your spouse will enjoy: their favorite drink, a handwritten card, or taking care of some small task they’ve been putting off for ages.
Exchange surprises on your date and share: “This week, you were really patient with me about… Thank you.”
Together, come up with a plan to show kindness to someone else this month, such as taking a lonely friend out for a meal.
Hold hands, read the first half of 1 Corinthians 13:4 together, and pray for each other.

lessons.title: Without Love, I Am Nothing
lessons.theme: However much we give, without love all that’s left is noise

v: If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal.
If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but don’t have love, I am nothing.
If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.

lessons.still: Be still and think about what you did for your family today. Don’t rush to grade yourself; just tell the Lord: “Lord, I’ve done a lot, but I want to know: is there love in any of it?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Giving without love is often self-ruled giving: I’ve done so much, so you must be grateful and you must notice me. When the focus is on myself, giving turns into collecting a debt. When we let Jesus reign, giving becomes simple again: for the Lord and for our spouse, not for my own record of merit.
lessons.jesus: Martha was busy serving Jesus, but she was frazzled inside and even complained about her sister. Jesus said gently, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed” (Luke 10:41–42). Jesus wasn’t dismissing her service; he was bringing Martha back to the heart behind it.
lessons.pray: Lord, we confess that we often do a great deal while our hearts have no love left, only weariness and scorekeeping. Forgive us for treating our giving as a record of merit. Put your love back into our hearts, so that every small thing we do for each other becomes a melody of love rather than noise. Amen.
teach: Picture a beautifully designed phone with a big screen and multiple cameras, but a dead battery. However good it looks, it can’t make a single call. The church in Corinth had many gifts, such as tongues, prophecy, and knowledge, yet they compared themselves with each other and split into factions. Right between two chapters on spiritual gifts, Paul placed this chapter, saying, “I show a most excellent way to you” (1 Corinthians 12:31). That most excellent way is love.

Paul says, “If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal” (1 Corinthians 13:1). A gong and a cymbal are loud, but they carry no melody. He goes on to say that even with all faith, even “If I give away all my goods to feed the poor... but don’t have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3). However impressive our outward actions, without love they are empty in God’s eyes.

This passage is very practical for couples. We may spend every day driving the kids around, cooking, working overtime, and paying bills, doing lots of “right things,” while our hearts are full of resentment and scorekeeping. What our spouse hears is not our giving, but the noise of gongs and cymbals. This week we’ll read the portrait of love line by line. The first step is to ask honestly: is there still love in my giving?
q: Of the things I’ve done for my family recently, which one has turned into “sounding brass or a clanging cymbal”?
Do I often keep a mental tally of how much I have given to this family?
talk: Of the things I do for our home, which one makes you feel most loved? Which one do you sense I do out of exhaustion or reluctance? Please tell me gently.
If our family life were a piece of music, would you say it sounds more like a melody or more like noise right now? How could we tune it?
acts: Pick one daily household chore and do it today with prayer and love
Tell your spouse: “Thank you for doing … for our family. I see it.”
Say one less complaint today
lessons.noon: “but don’t have love, I am nothing” — Lord, add your love to everything I do right now.

lessons.title: A Long Fuse
lessons.theme: Patience means being slow to anger, as God is

v: The LORD passed by before him, and proclaimed, “The LORD! The LORD, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud,

lessons.still: Take three deep breaths, each one a little slower than the last. Tell the Lord: “Lord, you have been so patient with me. Today, please put your long-suffering patience in my heart.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: A short fuse often comes from too big a “me”: my time, my standards, and my feelings must never be offended. The self-emptied have a longer fuse, because they remember that God’s patience with me far exceeds my patience with my spouse.
lessons.jesus: Philip had followed Jesus for so long, yet he still said, “Show us the Father.” Jesus answered, “Have I been with you such a long time, and do you not know me, Philip?” (John 14:9). There was a sigh in his voice, but he did not give up; he patiently taught once more. Jesus is our example of patience.
lessons.pray: Merciful and gracious God, thank you that you are slow to anger and so full of patience toward us. We confess that our fuses with each other are often too short, and we explode at the slightest spark. Holy Spirit, give us a quiet space between our anger and our reactions, so that your love can speak first. Amen.
teach: A firecracker has a fuse. With a short fuse, it explodes the moment it’s lit; with a long fuse, there’s still time to put the flame out after it’s lit. Paul says, “Love is patient” (1 Corinthians 13:4). In the original Greek, this is a verb that literally carries the sense of “being long-tempered,” bearing with others for a long time and being slow to anger. Patient people aren’t people without fire; they simply have a long fuse that leaves room for love.

This pattern comes from God himself. After Israel worshiped the golden calf, God proclaimed before Moses: “The LORD! The LORD, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth” (Exodus 34:6). In Hebrew, “slow to anger” pictures anger that is long in coming. Israel had just betrayed him, and yet this is how God introduced himself.

What tests our patience most in marriage is usually not the big things but the small, repeated ones: saying the same thing for the tenth time, seeing the same habit show up again. Patience is not pretending everything is fine; it is leaving a space between our anger and our reaction, so the Holy Spirit has a chance to speak. That space may be only three seconds, yet it often decides the direction of the whole conversation.
q: With which of my spouse’s small habits is my “fuse” especially short?
When I think about how long God has been patient with me, what do I feel?
talk: When I’m about to lose my temper, how do you think I could pause for three seconds first? Could we agree on a signal to remind each other?
In what area do you most appreciate my patience with you?
acts: When you feel like losing your temper today, pause for three seconds and say in your heart, “Lord”
Agree with your spouse on a gentle “time-out” signal
Write down one way God has been patient with you
lessons.noon: “a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger” — Lord, right now lengthen my fuse, and let love speak first.

lessons.title: Bearing Each Other’s Weaknesses
lessons.theme: Learning to accept our spouse’s weaknesses and habits rather than remake them

v: Now we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves.
Let each one of us please his neighbor for that which is good, to be building him up.
Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you, to the glory of God.

lessons.still: Think of one of your spouse’s habits that often makes you sigh. Don’t rush to pray “Lord, change them.” Instead, quietly say: “Lord, this is how you have accepted my weaknesses too.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Trying to remake my spouse to fit my standards is trying to take God’s place in doing his work in them. Let people be people, and let God be God: my part is to accept and to bear; God’s part is to change them. Humility inspires humility, and a person who feels accepted actually finds it easier to change.
lessons.jesus: The prophet described Jesus this way: “He won’t break a bruised reed. He won’t quench a smoking flax” (Matthew 12:20). When Jesus faced weak people, he did not snap them in two; he carefully lifted them up. He was gentle toward weakness, yet he never compromised with sin. This is the direction for how we learn patience.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for accepting us while we were still weak. Help us accept each other and bear each other’s weaknesses, instead of rushing to remake each other. And please protect everyone who is hurt or afraid in their marriage; give them safety, wisdom, and help. Amen.
teach: There was once a couple: the wife liked to squeeze the toothpaste from the end, while the husband always squeezed it from the middle. They argued over this little thing for years. Eventually the wife simply bought two tubes, one each, and they both laughed. Marriage is full of weaknesses and habits that aren’t sins, just differences. They are not enemies to be wiped out, but weights to be carried.

Paul says, “we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves” (Romans 15:1). To “bear” means to pick something up and carry it. He also says, “accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you” (Romans 15:7). Christ did not accept us after we got better, but while we were still weak. Acceptance doesn’t mean approving of everything; it means first welcoming the person in.

We need to be especially clear here: bearing with weakness does not mean putting up with harm. Physical, verbal, sexual, or financial violence and control are not “weaknesses,” and they are not something love is meant to tolerate. If you feel afraid or unsafe in your marriage, first protect your own safety and your children’s, and seek help from a pastor and from professionals. Seeking help is not a failure of patience; it is an expression of love and truth.
q: What “difference” in my spouse have I kept treating as a mistake to be corrected?
Which of my own weaknesses has my spouse been quietly bearing for a long time?
talk: Which of my little habits often requires patience from you? Please tell me in a lighthearted way.
Is there some small thing we keep tugging back and forth over that we could solve with a “two tubes of toothpaste” approach?
acts: Choose to smile rather than comment on one of your spouse’s little habits today
Tell your spouse: “Thank you for putting up with my…”
If you feel unsafe in your marriage, contact a trusted pastor or professional today
lessons.noon: “accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you” — Lord, right now I choose to accept my spouse just as you have accepted me.

lessons.title: Kindness Leads Us Home
lessons.theme: Kindness is actively doing good, and it changes people more than rebuke does

v: Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?
But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared,
not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit,

lessons.still: Recall how God once gently brought you back when you had stumbled. Quietly thank him: “Lord, it was your kindness that turned me around.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Trying to change my spouse through blame means taking the judge’s seat, and that is leaving our rightful place. God’s view is that kindness leads people to repentance. When I lay down the power of “I’m right and you’re wrong,” return to my rightful place as a servant, and actively treat my spouse well, God works in their heart.
lessons.jesus: The crowd wanted to stone a woman caught in adultery, but Jesus said, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more” (John 8:11). He did not take sin lightly, but he first protected her with kindness and then called her to a new life. Kindness and truth are perfectly joined in Jesus.
lessons.pray: Our Savior, thank you that your kindness and love came to us and saved us when we were least lovable. Forgive us for so often treating each other with blame. Make us warm like the sun, opening each other’s hearts by actively doing good, and let your kindness lead people home in our family. Amen.
teach: The North Wind and the Sun made a bet over who could get a traveler to take off his coat. The North Wind blew with all its might, and the traveler only wrapped his coat more tightly around himself; the Sun shone warmly, and the traveler took off his coat on his own. This fable is a lot like marriage: blame often makes people more defensive, while kindness helps them lower their guard. The harder we try to “blow” our spouse awake, the more they tend to wrap themselves up.

Paul asks, “do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?” (Romans 2:4). The word WEB renders “goodness” here is God’s kindness. God’s way of changing us is not to condemn first, but to show kindness first. In 1 Corinthians 13:4, “kind” is also a verb, meaning to actively treat others well and do what is truly good for them. Patience is not exploding; kindness goes a step further: it takes the initiative to do good.

Titus describes what we once were: “hateful, and hating one another” (Titus 3:3), and then says, “when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared... he saved us” (Titus 3:4–5). We are all people changed by kindness. At home, a glass of warm water, a word like “Thanks for all your hard work,” or an understanding look can often open our spouse’s heart more than ten good arguments.
q: When my spouse does something wrong, do I usually respond more like the North Wind or the Sun?
What act of God’s kindness once changed my heart?
talk: When you’ve done something wrong or you’re in a bad mood, what could I do that would make you feel most kindly treated?
Was there a recent time when I used blame instead of kindness? I’d like to apologize, and I’d like to hear how you felt.
acts: Today, take the initiative to do something good for your spouse that they didn’t ask for
Swap one critical comment you want to make for an understanding one
Do a small act of kindness for the family member you find hardest to treat kindly
lessons.noon: “the goodness of God leads you to repentance” — Lord, right now I choose to treat my family with your kindness.

lessons.title: Always at the King’s Table
lessons.theme: Kind love prepares a place for the other person

v: The king said, “Is there not yet any of Saul’s house, that I may show the kindness of God to him?” Ziba said to the king, “Jonathan still has a son, who is lame in his feet.”
The king said to him, “Where is he?” Ziba said to the king, “Behold, he is in the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, in Lo Debar.”
Then King David sent and brought him out of the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, from Lo Debar.
Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, came to David, fell on his face, and showed respect. David said, “Mephibosheth?” He answered, “Behold, your servant!”

David said to him, “Don’t be afraid, for I will surely show you kindness for Jonathan your father’s sake, and will restore to you all the land of Saul your father. You will eat bread at my table continually.”

lessons.still: Imagine being invited to sit at a long table, where the host personally pulls out a chair for you. Look back over this week: love in our giving, a long fuse, bearing weaknesses, kindness. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, thank you for preparing a place for me.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: David showed kindness because he remembered a covenant, not because of what the other person had to offer. Marriage, too, is a covenant, not a transaction. Relationships matter more than things, and people matter more than tasks: a home where a weak person can sit down and feel safe is a home being built as a household that belongs to God.
lessons.jesus: When the disciples were so busy they didn’t even have time to eat, Jesus said, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile” (Mark 6:31). Jesus saw how tired people were and took the initiative to make space for them to rest. This is what Jesus’ kindness looks like: not only making demands, but showing care.
lessons.pray: King of covenant love, thank you for seeking us because of your covenant, so that weak people like us can always eat at your table. Make our home a table of kindness, where each other’s weaknesses have a place to rest. May we never give up in patience, and may we actively do good in kindness, showing your love. Amen.
teach: After David became king, he asked a remarkable question: “Is there not yet any of Saul’s house, that I may show the kindness of God to him?” (2 Samuel 9:3). By the custom of the time, a new king would often wipe out the descendants of the previous dynasty. But David remembered his covenant with Jonathan and went looking on his own initiative. The word translated “kindness” here is the Hebrew word for covenant love: faithfulness and goodness that flow from a covenant.

The one they found was Mephibosheth, who at five years old had fallen while fleeing and was lame for the rest of his life. When he came before David, he fell on his face, terrified. Yet David said, “Don’t be afraid,” and also, “You will eat bread at my table continually” (2 Samuel 9:7). Kindness is not just helping out once; it is keeping a lasting place at your own table for someone who is weak.

This week we have learned about patience and kindness. Patience means not giving up; kindness means actively doing good. Mephibosheth’s legs didn’t get better, but he always ate at the king’s table. In marriage, our spouse also carries their own “lameness”: past wounds, the limits of their personality. Love doesn’t wait for them to be healed before accepting them; it lets them know: at this family’s table, there will always be a place for you.
q: What “lameness” in my spouse do I keep hoping will get better before I’m willing to accept them?
Of this week’s lessons on patience and kindness, where does God most want to work in me?
talk: In our home, when do you most feel that you “have a place” and are welcome?
Could we do something together to make our dinner table more of a place of kindness? For example, putting our phones away at meals and checking in with each other.
acts: At dinner tonight, put your phone away and really look at your spouse as you talk
Tell your spouse: “Whatever happens, there will always be a place for you in this family.”
Memorize the first half of 1 Corinthians 13:4
lessons.noon: “You will eat bread at my table continually” — Lord, right now I thank you for the place you have prepared for me.

11.title: Love Does Not Seek Its Own Way

mem.t: doesn’t behave itself inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil;

s: Find a quiet little café. Each take a sheet of paper and privately write down one “old account” you’ve been holding on to in your heart and haven’t truly let go of. You don’t need to show it to each other.
Read Psalm 103:12 together. Each of you silently hand that paper over to the Lord in your heart, then tear the papers into pieces together and throw them away.
Take turns saying: “This week, for your good, I want to…”
On the way home, sincerely congratulate your spouse on a recent achievement or effort.

lessons.title: Love Doesn’t Envy: Rejoicing in Your Success
lessons.theme: Love can truly rejoice in our spouse’s good instead of secretly comparing

v: As they came, when David returned from the slaughter of the Philistine, the women came out of all the cities of Israel, singing and dancing, to meet King Saul with tambourines, with joy, and with instruments of music.
The women sang to one another as they played, and said, “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.”
Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him. He said, “They have credited David with ten thousands, and they have only credited me with thousands. What can he have more but the kingdom?”
Saul watched David from that day and forward.
Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep.

lessons.still: Think of a recent moment when your spouse was praised or recognized. Honestly examine what your first reaction was in that moment. Tell the Lord: “Lord, search my heart for any comparison and envy.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Envy is the comparison of the self-ruled life: “Why them and not me?” The focus is on myself. The self-emptied know their place before God and don’t need to compete with their spouse for first place. When we let Jesus receive all the glory, we don’t have to fight each other for the applause.
lessons.jesus: When the seventy disciples returned from their mission and joyfully reported the results, “In that same hour, Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit” (Luke 10:21). Jesus did not feel threatened by his disciples’ fruitfulness; instead he rejoiced for them and gave thanks to the Father. He is our example of truly rejoicing in other people’s success.
lessons.pray: Lord, search out the hidden comparison and envy in our hearts. We confess that we sometimes treat our spouse as a rival instead of a partner on the same team. Heal our insecurity, and help us, like Jonathan, to truly rejoice in each other’s good, giving the glory to you together in each other’s successes. Amen.
teach: When King Saul returned to the city after a victory, the women sang: “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands” (1 Samuel 18:7). It should have been a day of national celebration, yet “Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him,” and “Saul watched David from that day and forward” (1 Samuel 18:8–9). One comparison planted a lifetime of envy in his heart.

In marriage, envy often shows up in disguise: my spouse gets promoted, and I say congratulations while feeling sour inside; friends all praise the wife’s cooking, and the husband feels outshone; the children cling more to one parent, and the other quietly feels let down. The root of envy is treating our spouse as a competitor rather than a teammate on the same side.

The same chapter shows us another person: Jonathan. As the crown prince, he had more reason than anyone to envy David, yet he “loved him as his own soul” (1 Samuel 18:3). Paul says, “Rejoice with those who rejoice” (Romans 12:15). Truly rejoicing in someone else’s good is sometimes harder than weeping with those who weep. Husband and wife are one, so my spouse’s success is our success.
q: What recent good thing in my spouse’s life did I congratulate them on while feeling a little sour inside?
In some areas, have I been treating my spouse as a competitor?
talk: Is there something worth celebrating in your life lately that I haven’t properly rejoiced with you about?
How could we build a habit of “celebrating each other” at home? For example, naming one thing the other person did really well each week.
acts: Today, specifically praise one thing your spouse did well
Pray wholeheartedly once for one of your spouse’s dreams or goals
When you notice yourself comparing, immediately turn it into thanks to God
lessons.noon: “Rejoice with those who rejoice” — Lord, right now I choose to rejoice sincerely in my spouse’s good.

lessons.title: Love Doesn’t Brag and Isn’t Proud
lessons.theme: Love doesn’t prove itself by lifting itself up; love builds others up

v: “Two men went up into the temple to pray; one was a Pharisee, and the other was a tax collector.
The Pharisee stood and prayed by himself like this: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men: extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector.
I fast twice a week. I give tithes of all that I get.’
But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his chest, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.”
Now concerning things sacrificed to idols: We know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.

lessons.still: Be still for a moment and imagine yourself standing before God, with no need to report your achievements or prove anything. Softly say, “God, be merciful to me.” Rest in those words.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride means leaving our rightful place and lifting ourselves up, wanting to sit in God’s seat and judge others. Humility means returning to our rightful place and admitting that we too need grace. Pride provokes pride, and couples end up competing over who is more right; humility inspires humility, and one “I was wrong” often brings back another: “I wasn’t right either.”
lessons.jesus: Jesus, the Son of God, said, “But I don’t seek my own glory. There is one who seeks and judges” (John 8:50). He had no need to promote himself, because he rested in the Father’s approval. Jesus shows us that true security frees us from the need to brag.
lessons.pray: God, be merciful to us. We confess that we often lift ourselves up and try to prove to our spouse that we are right. Pop the balloon of pride in our hearts, bring us back to our rightful place, and make us willing to say “Thank you,” “You’re right,” and “I was wrong.” Let our words become love that builds each other up. Amen.
teach: The bigger you blow up a balloon, the more impressive it looks, yet it holds nothing but air, and a single pin can pop it. Paul says love “is not proud” (1 Corinthians 13:4). The Greek word means “puffed up” or inflated, the same word Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 8:1, where he says, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Corinthians 8:1). Pride inflates the self; love builds other people up.

Jesus told a parable about two men who went up to the temple to pray. The Pharisee said, “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men” (Luke 18:11), and went on to list his record of fasting and giving. But the tax collector stood far off and said, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13). Jesus said it was the tax collector who went home justified.

In marriage, bragging often hides in little sentences: “If it weren’t for me, this family would have…” “See? I told you so.” “I know better than you.” These may even be true, but like the Pharisee’s prayer, they put me up high and my spouse down low. Love that doesn’t brag is willing to say, “Thank you,” “You’re right,” and “I was wrong this time.”
q: What “bragging sentence” do I say most often to my spouse?
In what area do I feel I “know better” than my spouse, and so often look down on their opinion?
talk: Is there something I often say that makes you feel looked down on? Please tell me gently. I want to hear it.
In our home, what words do the most to “build you up” and give you strength?
acts: Say “You’re right” to your spouse at least once today
When you catch yourself about to say “I told you so,” swallow the words
Say one specific thing that builds your spouse up
lessons.noon: “love builds up” — Lord, right now help me build others up in love rather than lift myself up.

lessons.title: Love Doesn’t Seek Its Own Way
lessons.theme: Love faces outward and looks first to our spouse’s needs

v: Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good.
each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.
Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus,

lessons.still: Think about the pressures or needs your spouse may be facing today. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, open my eyes today to see not only my own concerns, but theirs too.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: When the self-ruled make a decision, the first question is “What’s in it for me?” The self-emptied first ask, “Is this good for us, and for my spouse?” This is not losing yourself; it is emptying yourself as Christ did, and in doing so gaining a greater life and a deeper oneness.
lessons.jesus: At the Last Supper, Jesus “arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist” (John 13:4), and washed his disciples’ feet himself. This was a servant’s job, and none of the disciples was willing to do it. Jesus was Lord, yet he did not seek his own way; he bent down to serve.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are Lord, yet you bent down to wash your disciples’ feet. We confess that we often look only to our own concerns and keep the good things for ourselves. Give us your heart, make us willing to look first to each other’s needs, to be considerate in small things and gentle in our words, and fill our home with the love of serving one another. Amen.
teach: Picture two people sharing one umbrella in the rain. If each pulls the umbrella toward themselves, both end up half soaked; if each pushes it toward the other, the umbrella ends up in the middle and both stay covered. Love “doesn’t seek its own way” (1 Corinthians 13:5); it is the act of pushing the umbrella toward the other person.

In the same letter, Paul says, “Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good” (1 Corinthians 10:24). He also urges the believers in Philippi: “each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others” (Philippians 2:4). Notice the words “not just” and “also.” Paul does not tell us to ignore ourselves entirely, only not to look out for ourselves alone. The eyes of love turn from “me” to “us.”

The same verse also says love “doesn’t behave itself inappropriately” (1 Corinthians 13:5), which carries the sense of rude or unbecoming conduct. Home is where we most easily become careless with people: a sharp tone, no regard for how the other feels. Love that doesn’t seek its own way shows care in small things: handing over the remote, saving the last piece for them, and even when tired, first asking how their day went. This is what it means to “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5).
q: In which small matter in our home do I always pull the “umbrella” toward myself?
Is the tone I use with my spouse more careless than the tone I use with outsiders?
talk: Is there something lately where you wish I would consider your needs more? Please tell me one specific thing.
Could we each choose one small thing at home this week where we deliberately “push the umbrella toward the other”?
acts: Today, give up to your spouse some small thing or choice you would have liked
Ask your spouse: “Is there anything I can help you with today?”
Watch your tone, and treat your family with the courtesy you’d show a guest
lessons.noon: “each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others” — Lord, right now open my eyes to see my spouse’s needs.

lessons.title: Love Is Not Provoked
lessons.theme: Before I’m provoked, let God ask me: Is it right for you to be angry?

v: The discretion of a man makes him slow to anger. It is his glory to overlook an offense.
But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry.

He prayed to the LORD, and said, “Please, LORD, wasn’t this what I said when I was still in my own country? Therefore I hurried to flee to Tarshish, for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and you relent of doing harm.
Therefore now, LORD, take, I beg you, my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.”
The LORD said, “Is it right for you to be angry?”

lessons.still: Think about the last time you lost your temper with your spouse. Don’t condemn yourself; just quietly bring that picture to the Lord and hear him gently ask: “Is it right for you to be angry?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Being quick to anger usually means “I” have been offended: my pride, my plans, my rights. Jonah’s anger came because God didn’t do things his way. Let God be God; when we admit he is wiser than we are, our anger loses the ground it stands on.
lessons.jesus: When a Samaritan village would not welcome Jesus, James and John wanted to call down fire from heaven. But Jesus “turned and rebuked them,” saying, “For the Son of Man didn’t come to destroy men’s lives, but to save them” (Luke 9:55–56). When Jesus was rejected, he was not provoked; he simply went on to another village.
lessons.pray: Gracious and merciful God, you are slow to anger, yet we often explode at the slightest touch. Give us discretion to see the weariness and pain behind each other’s behavior. When anger rises, gently ask us: Is it right for you to be angry? Make us willing to stop and let your peace rule first. Amen.
teach: When a pressure cooker’s valve keeps hissing, it means the pressure inside is already high. Love “is not provoked” (1 Corinthians 13:5); the original word means not easily stirred to anger. Paul isn’t saying love never feels anger, but that love doesn’t explode at the slightest touch. Often when we blow up at our spouse, it isn’t really about that small thing; the pressure inside was already full.

When Jonah saw the people of Nineveh repent and God hold back disaster, “it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry” (Jonah 4:1). He even said to God, “I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger” (Jonah 4:2). Jonah knew God was slow to anger, yet he himself was quick to anger. God didn’t argue with him; he asked only one question: “Is it right for you to be angry?” (Jonah 4:4)

Proverbs says, “The discretion of a man makes him slow to anger. It is his glory to overlook an offense” (Proverbs 19:11). Discretion means seeing more deeply and further ahead. When we see the weariness, fear, or pain behind our spouse’s behavior, our anger cools. Next time we are about to get angry, we can let God ask us the same question, giving ourselves a chance to look again from God’s point of view.
q: The last time I got angry at my spouse, what part of me was really offended?
What pressures are building up in my inner “pressure cooker” right now that I haven’t yet handed to God?
talk: When I’m angry, what kind of response helps me calm down the most? What kind of response makes things worse?
Could we agree on a way that, when one of us is about to blow up, we pause first, each pray, and talk again a little later?
acts: When you feel like getting angry today, first ask yourself: “Is it right for me to be angry?”
Write down one pressure that has been building up in your heart, and hand it to God
Agree with your spouse on a way to “pause and talk later”
lessons.noon: “The discretion of a man makes him slow to anger” — Lord, right now give me discretion to see the needs behind people’s hearts.

lessons.title: Love Takes No Account of Evil
lessons.theme: Love doesn’t dig up old accounts, because God has wiped our account clean

v: He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us for our iniquities.
For as the heavens are high above the earth, so great is his loving kindness toward those who fear him.
As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us.
Who is a God like you, who pardons iniquity, and passes over the disobedience of the remnant of his heritage? He doesn’t retain his anger forever, because he delights in loving kindness.
He will again have compassion on us. He will tread our iniquities under foot. You will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.

lessons.still: Look back over this week: not envying, not bragging, not seeking our own way, not being provoked. Now imagine God picking up the ledger full of your wrongs and throwing it into the deep sea. Quietly thank him: “Lord, you no longer remember my sins.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The ledger in my heart keeps me permanently in the creditor’s seat, free to demand payment from my spouse at any time; that is the power of the self-ruled life. Handing the ledger to God means laying down the authority to judge, and letting God be God. Only the self-emptied are truly free, and they set their spouse free as well.
lessons.jesus: Nailed to the cross, in the greatest agony, Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). He did not keep a list of everyone who mocked him; he interceded for them. Jesus is our highest example of taking no account of evil.
lessons.pray: God who forgives us, thank you for not dealing with us according to our sins, and for casting our sins into the depths of the sea. Help us hand the ledgers in our hearts over to you, to stop dragging up the past, and to stop using it as a weapon. And please protect those who are hurt in their marriages; give them safety, courage, and help. Amen.
teach: Many shops keep a ledger that records exactly how much each customer owes, entry by entry. Paul says love “takes no account of evil” (1 Corinthians 13:5). The original word is an accounting term meaning to keep a record, to enter something in the books. What hurts most in a couple’s argument is often not today’s issue but the line: “You always do this! That time three years ago…” Dragging up the past means opening the ledger in our hearts.

The psalmist says, “He has not dealt with us according to our sins... As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us” (Psalm 103:10–12). Micah also says of God’s people, “You will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea” (Micah 7:19). God hasn’t forgotten; he has chosen never to bring them out again to collect on them. Taking no account of evil is also a choice: no longer using old accounts as weapons.

But taking no account of evil does not mean pretending nothing happened, and it certainly does not mean staying in danger. If your spouse keeps hurting or controlling you physically, verbally, sexually, or financially, that is not something to silently “not take account of.” Forgiveness means giving up the right to revenge, yet you can still set boundaries, protect your safety, and seek help from a pastor and from professionals. Safety comes first, and that too is love.
q: What old account am I still holding in my heart that I often bring out when we argue?
Of my sins that God has thrown into the deep sea, which one am I most grateful for?
talk: Could we agree that when we argue, we’ll talk only about the one issue in front of us, and stop saying “You always” and “You never”?
Of this week’s five “love doesn’t” lessons, in which area do you think our family most needs to grow? If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down what you’d like to say to them.
acts: Today, when you argue or feel upset, talk only about the one issue in front of you
Write down one old account you can’t let go of, pray over it, then tear it up
Memorize 1 Corinthians 13:5
lessons.noon: “You will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea” — Lord, right now I hand the old accounts in my heart over to you too.

mem.t: bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things.

date.t: A Four-Season Map of Our Marriage
s: Take a sheet of paper and divide it into four boxes labeled spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Together, think back over the seasons your marriage has passed through, and each write a few memorable events in the matching boxes.
Take turns sharing: “In that winter, what kept us from letting go?” Notice God’s faithfulness in every season.
Each name one hope for the future, write it on the back of the paper, and pray over it together.
Read 1 Corinthians 13:4–8a aloud together, then read it again replacing “love” with “the Lord Jesus,” and ask him to live out this kind of love in you.

lessons.title: Bears All Things: The Roof Over Our Home
lessons.theme: Love is like a roof, sheltering our spouse from wind and rain, but never covering up harm

v: Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all wrongs.
And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins.

lessons.still: Imagine sitting at home on a rainy night, listening to the rain drum on the roof while you stay dry and warm. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, thank you for being my shelter. Make me a shelter for my family too.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Exposing our spouse’s faults is often a way to prove “I’m better,” and that is the pride of the self-ruled life. Self-emptied love is willing to bear the weight and protect our spouse’s dignity, because we are one; their shame is my shame. Relationships matter more than saving face, and people matter more than being right.
lessons.jesus: When the soldiers came to arrest Jesus, he stepped forward and said, “If therefore you seek me, let these go their way” (John 18:8). Jesus placed himself in front of his disciples, protecting them like a roof. True bearing means covering the ones we love with ourselves.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for being our shelter and covering our many sins. Make us a roof for each other, never exposing each other’s faults, but shielding each other from the storm in times of weakness. And please protect everyone who is being harmed in their home; give them courage to speak up, and lead them to people who can help. Amen.
teach: One of the most important parts of a house is the roof. When storms come, the roof doesn’t keep a tally of every raindrop; it simply keeps the rain out so the people inside can sleep in peace. Paul says love “bears all things” (1 Corinthians 13:7). The original word carries the sense of covering and bearing up, close to the image of a roof. Love is like a roof: when someone in the family is weak, it shields them from the storm outside.

Proverbs says, “Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all wrongs” (Proverbs 10:12). Peter also says, “above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8). Covering means not broadcasting our spouse’s weaknesses, not exposing their faults to friends and family or on social media, and not belittling them in front of the children. Love protects our spouse’s reputation as if it were our own.

But a roof keeps out the rain outside; it doesn’t hide a fire inside the house. Bearing all things does not mean keeping secrets for violence, affairs, addiction, or any ongoing harm. If there is physical, verbal, sexual, or financial violence and control in the home, it is not something to be covered; it needs to be brought into the light and dealt with. Please put safety first and seek help from a pastor and from professionals. This is not betrayal; it is true love.
q: Have I ever told others about my spouse’s weaknesses or embarrassing moments? What was I hoping to gain at the time?
How has God covered my wrongs and kept me from being shamed in front of others?
talk: Was there a time when I talked about you in front of others and it made you uncomfortable? Please tell me. I want to learn to protect you better.
Is there a pressure or weakness you’re facing lately that you’d like me to quietly help carry?
acts: Say something good about your spouse in front of others today
Stop complaining about your spouse on social media or in chats
Quietly take on one task to share a pressure your spouse is facing
lessons.noon: “love covers a multitude of sins” — Lord, right now make me a shelter for my family.

lessons.title: Believes All Things: Seeing What God Is Doing
lessons.theme: Love is not naive; it believes in God’s good work in our spouse

v: being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.

So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.”
He said to him again a second time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Tend my sheep.”

He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you have affection for me?” Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time, “Do you have affection for me?” He said to him, “Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.

lessons.still: Think about what your spouse was like when you first met, and what they are like now. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, what good work have you done in them that I haven’t noticed?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Labeling my spouse with “That’s just how they are” is me drawing conclusions in God’s place. Let God be God: admit that he understands my spouse better than I do and is more able to change them than I am. When our focus is on Jesus, we can turn from disappointment to hope, and from judgment to intercession.
lessons.jesus: Before Peter ever fell, Jesus told him, “but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers” (Luke 22:32). Jesus knew Peter would fail, yet he already believed Peter would turn back. That is love that believes all things.
lessons.pray: God who completes every good work, thank you that you have never given up on us, nor on our spouse. Remove the labels and judgments from our hearts, and give us eyes of faith to see the work you are doing in each other. Let us strengthen each other with “I believe in you,” and wait together for you to complete your work. Amen.
teach: A sculptor looks at a rough block of stone. Others see only stone, but he already sees the statue inside. Love “believes all things” (1 Corinthians 13:7). That doesn’t mean love is naive and believes anything; it means love is willing to see people with the eyes of faith, seeing not only who they are now, but also who God is shaping them to become.

Paul says, “being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). Notice that the focus of Paul’s confidence is not people but God. Believing in our spouse doesn’t mean believing they will never fail again; it means believing God hasn’t given up on them and is still at work in them. This lets us keep faith in our spouse even in disappointment.

Peter denied the Lord three times, yet after the resurrection Jesus asked him three times whether he loved him, and three times entrusted him with the charge: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17). Jesus didn’t label Peter “unreliable” because of his failure; instead he believed in him again and entrusted him with a task. Love that believes all things gives our spouse the chance to start again, and rebuilds them with three words: “I believe in you.”
q: Have I ever put a label on my spouse, such as “They’ll just never change”?
What good work has God already done in my spouse that I can be thankful for?
talk: In what area would you most like me to have more faith in you?
Name one change you have seen God make in each other, and tell your spouse: “I believe God will keep completing it.”
acts: Tell your spouse today: “I believe God has a good plan for you.”
Write down three ways your spouse has grown in recent years, and thank God
Tear off one negative label you have stuck on your spouse in your heart
lessons.noon: “he who began a good work in you will complete it” — Lord, right now I believe you will complete your work in our home.

lessons.title: Hopes All Things: A Door in the Valley of Trouble
lessons.theme: God can turn the valley of trouble in a marriage into a door of hope

v: “Therefore behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her.
I will give her vineyards from there, and the valley of Achor for a door of hope; and she will respond there as in the days of her youth, and as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt.
Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that you may abound in hope in the power of the Holy Spirit.

lessons.still: Think of a low point your marriage has passed through, or is passing through now. You don’t need to hurry out of it; just quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, in this valley, open a door for us.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: We lose hope when our eyes are fixed on our spouse or our circumstances. The earthly view sees only the valley; the heavenly view sees the door. Moving from the temporary to the eternal, with our focus on Jesus, we can keep preparing for spring even in winter.
lessons.jesus: Jairus’ daughter had died and everyone was weeping, but Jesus said, “The child is not dead, but is asleep” (Mark 5:39). People laughed at him, but he took the child by the hand and raised her up. Where everyone else saw only despair, Jesus saw hope.
lessons.pray: God of hope, thank you that you can turn the valley of trouble into a door of hope. We place the low points and disappointments of our marriage in your hands. Speak tenderly to us in the wilderness, fill our hearts with joy and peace as we trust in you, and let us overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit. Amen.
teach: In winter, a tree loses all its leaves and looks dead. But anyone who knows gardening knows that the roots are quietly gathering strength underground, waiting for spring. Love “hopes all things” (1 Corinthians 13:7). It means believing, even in the winter of a marriage, that spring will come, because our hope is in God, not in our circumstances.

The book of Hosea uses marriage to describe the relationship between God and Israel. The people had abandoned God, yet God said, “I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her,” and “I will give her... the valley of Achor for a door of hope” (Hosea 2:14–15). “Achor” means “trouble”; it was the place where Israel was punished because of Achan’s sin. God actually turns the most painful valley into a door of hope.

Paul blesses the church: “may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing” (Romans 15:13). The source of hope is God. Hope in marriage is not cheerfully pretending there are no problems; it is fixing our eyes, in the midst of problems, on the God who raises the dead. For many couples, a low point later became the starting point of a deeper connection.
q: Is there a “valley of Achor” in our marriage that I hardly dare to hope about anymore?
Is my hope right now fixed more on my spouse changing, or on God?
talk: Think back to a low point we went through. How did God later open a door in it?
What do you hope for our marriage in the coming year? If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down the hopes you hold for them and for your family.
acts: Write down something you have given up hoping for, and hand it to God again
Tell your spouse: “I have hope for our future.”
Remember a door God opened in one of your low points, and thank him for it
lessons.noon: “the valley of Achor for a door of hope” — Lord, right now open a door of hope for us in our valley.

lessons.title: Endures All Things: Waiting for the Early and Late Rain
lessons.theme: Love can stand firm under heavy loads, like a farmer waiting for the harvest

v: Be patient therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receives the early and late rain.
You also be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.
Jacob served seven years for Rachel. They seemed to him but a few days, for the love he had for her.

lessons.still: Picture a farmer standing at the edge of his field. The seed is sown, but nothing has broken the surface yet. He doesn’t anxiously dig up the soil; he simply waits quietly. Tell the Lord: “Lord, teach me to wait for you like this in my marriage too.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: We lose patience when we want to harvest on our own timetable; enduring all things means letting God be in charge of time. When we live from the heart by the Spirit, we have lasting strength; when we live from the head by ourselves, we easily start counting the cost and give up too soon.
lessons.jesus: In the Garden of Gethsemane, Jesus prayed in anguish, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). He did not run from the burden; under its weight he surrendered to the Father and walked the road to the cross to the end. This is love that endures all things.
lessons.pray: Lord, you are the God who holds time in your hands. We confess that we often want to see change on our own timetable, and we lose heart when it doesn’t come. Strengthen our hearts, so that like a farmer waiting for the early and late rain, we keep being faithful in small things. Let love give our waiting meaning, and keep us standing firm under heavy loads. Amen.
teach: In Week 10 we read that love “is patient,” which is about being slow to anger with people. Here, “endures all things” (1 Corinthians 13:7) uses a different word, which in the original carries the sense of standing firm under a heavy load and holding on to the end. The first is like a long fuse; the second is like a bridge pier that stays in place however hard the current pounds it. Marriage needs both kinds of patience.

James says, “the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receives the early and late rain” (James 5:7). A farmer can’t make the rain come early, but he can keep plowing, weeding, and waiting. The winter of a marriage is like this too: some changes can’t be seen in a week or two. What we can do is keep being faithful in small things, trusting that God will send the rain in his time.

Jacob served seven years to marry Rachel, and the Bible says, “They seemed to him but a few days, for the love he had for her” (Genesis 29:20). Love changed how the time felt. That doesn’t mean the waiting wasn’t hard; it means love gave the waiting meaning. Love that endures all things isn’t gritting your teeth and hanging on; it holds on because it sees that the other person is worth it. But please remember: endurance never means anyone should stay in violence or danger.
q: In my marriage, what am I expecting to change “quickly”? Have I given God time?
Is my endurance more like gritting my teeth and hanging on, or holding on because I see it’s worth it?
talk: Is there something in our marriage that we need to wait for patiently together? How can we encourage each other while we wait?
At what moment did my patience with you make you feel loved?
acts: Write down one thing that calls for patient waiting, and pray about it every day
Today, keep being faithful in one small thing without asking about the results
Tell your spouse: “Thank you for being so patient with me all along.”
lessons.noon: “You also be patient. Establish your hearts” — Lord, right now strengthen my heart to keep loving while I wait.

lessons.title: Love Never Fails
lessons.theme: Everything else will pass away; only love remains forever

v: Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will be done away with. Where there are various languages, they will cease. Where there is knowledge, it will be done away with.
For we know in part and we prophesy in part;
but when that which is complete has come, then that which is partial will be done away with.
When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I felt as a child, I thought as a child. Now that I have become a man, I have put away childish things.
For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I will know fully, even as I was also fully known.
But now faith, hope, and love remain—these three. The greatest of these is love.

lessons.still: Look back over these four weeks: the source of love; patience and kindness; not seeking our own way; bearing, believing, hoping, and enduring all things. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, I can’t do any of this love on my own, but you are love. Live it out in me.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Our love fails because human love is limited; God’s love never fails because God is limitless. Self-emptied does not mean empty; it means entering the limitless and living out of the limitless. When we stop loving in our own strength and let Christ love through us, a limited husband and wife can live out a love that never fails.
lessons.jesus: Before the Last Supper, John describes Jesus this way: “having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John 13:1). The disciples were about to desert him, yet he loved them to the end: to the cross, and forever. Jesus himself is the love that never fails.
lessons.pray: Love that never fails, we thank you, for you are love. We confess that we cannot live out this kind of love on our own, but you love us to the end. Dwell in our home, so that our patience, kindness, bearing, believing, and hoping all come from you. May our marriage become a testimony of your love until the day we see you face to face. Amen.
teach: When we got married, we received many gifts: the appliances will wear out, the photos will yellow, even the house will grow old. But Paul says, “Love never fails” (1 Corinthians 13:8). Prophecy, tongues, and knowledge, the gifts the Corinthians were so proud of, “will be done away with,” but love will not. Love is the only thing we can carry into eternity.

Paul uses two pictures. One is a child growing up: “Now that I have become a man, I have put away childish things” (1 Corinthians 13:11). The other is a mirror: “For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12). Ancient mirrors were polished bronze, and the image was blurry. Today our knowledge of God and of our spouse is limited, but one day we will see face to face and know fully.

Finally Paul sums it up: “But now faith, hope, and love remain—these three. The greatest of these is love” (1 Corinthians 13:13). Over these four weeks, we started from the source of love and learned the shape of love line by line. Perhaps we have discovered that only Jesus has ever fully lived out these descriptions of love. So the practice of love is not trying hard to imitate it, but letting the Love that never fails live in our home.
q: Of these four weeks on the nature of love, which verse has most changed how I see love?
If I replace “love” in 1 Corinthians 13:4–7 with my own name, which line can I hardly bear to read? I want to hand it to the Lord.
talk: Over these four weeks, in what specific way have you seen my love grow? Please tell me.
If our family were to choose one “family motto of love” from 1 Corinthians 13, which line would you choose? Why?
acts: Choose a “family motto of love” with your spouse, write it down, and post it in your home
Read 1 Corinthians 13:4–7 aloud, replacing “love” with “Jesus”
Memorize 1 Corinthians 13:7
lessons.noon: “Love never fails” — Lord, right now let your never-failing love live in our home.
