13.title: The Fruit of the Spirit (1): Love

mem.t: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.

s: Go for a stroll together through an orchard, a market, or the fruit aisle of a supermarket. Each pick one fruit and share which of your spouse’s strengths it reminds you of.
When you get home, draw a tree on a sheet of paper and write “2, 0, 9” on it. Each write down one fruit you saw the other bear this week.
Recite Galatians 5:22–23 together, then take turns saying: “For your sake, I am willing to let the Holy Spirit bear the fruit of love in me.”
Hold hands and pray, asking the Lord to make your home a garden full of fruit.

lessons.title: One Fruit, Nine Flavors
lessons.theme: The fruit of the Spirit is one life, not nine assignments

v: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith,
gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts.
If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.

lessons.still: Be still and picture a fruit tree quietly growing in the sunshine. It isn’t straining, yet it bears fruit naturally. Tell the Lord: “Holy Spirit, today I won’t rely on my own effort. I want to live in you and let you bear fruit in me.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: We often try to “improve ourselves,” adding a little patience and a little gentleness to the old self, and we only grow more tired. The nine flavors of fruit are not character traits that the self-ruled build through effort; they are the life that grows naturally when the self-emptied let the Holy Spirit lead. Change your mindset and your life will change: shift from “I have to achieve this” to “Holy Spirit, bear this fruit in me.”
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19). Every day the Son of God lived on earth, he lived in connection with the Father. Jesus is our example: fruit is not something we generate on our own; it flows out of an intimate relationship with the Father.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, thank you for living in us. We confess that we often try to become better on our own, and the harder we try, the more tired we become. Today we hand our old selves over to the cross. Bear your whole fruit in us: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control, and make our home your garden. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: Starting this week, we’ll spend nine weeks on “the fruit of the Spirit at home.” First, notice one detail: Paul speaks of “the fruit of the Spirit” (Galatians 5:22), and in the original, “fruit” is singular. Not nine fruits, but one fruit with nine flavors, like an orange with several segments that all belong to one orange. Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith (or faithfulness), gentleness, and self-control are nine facets of one and the same life.

This matters. If we treat the nine as nine assignments, we’ll pick the ones we’re good at and let ourselves off the hook for the ones we lack: “I’m very patient; I’m just not very gentle.” But one fruit is whole. It isn’t a report card we piece together; it is what the life of Christ looks like as it grows in us. Jesus said, “I am the vine. You are the branches” (John 15:5). A branch doesn’t have to strain to squeeze out fruit; it only has to remain in the vine.

Paul continues: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts” (Galatians 5:24). The fruit grows after the cross: once the old self has been put to death, the life of the Spirit has room. So Paul urges us, “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit” (Galatians 5:25). Home is the most real place for this fruit to grow.
q: Of the nine flavors, which one do I often comfort myself by saying “I already have that”? Which one do I rarely face?
At home lately, have I more often been “straining in my own strength” or “walking by the Spirit”?
talk: Read through the nine flavors. Which one do you think our family tastes most often right now? Which one is most lacking?
If our home were a fruit tree, what kind of fruit would you hope people taste when they walk into our home a year from now?
acts: Copy Galatians 5:22–23 onto a card and place it by the dinner table
When you feel impatient today, pray silently: “Holy Spirit, bear your fruit.”
This evening, tell your spouse about one fruit you saw in them today
lessons.noon: “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit” — Holy Spirit, right now I’m not relying on myself; guide my words and reactions.

lessons.title: My Spouse Is My Most Important “2”
lessons.theme: To love our neighbor as ourselves, we start with the person right beside us

v: For you, brothers, were called for freedom. Only don’t use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love be servants to one another.
For the whole law is fulfilled in one word, in this: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
But if you bite and devour one another, be careful that you don’t consume one another.

lessons.still: Close your eyes and think of the people you are connected to today, letting them come to mind one by one. Finally, let your thoughts rest on your spouse’s face. Gently tell the Lord: “Lord, thank you for placing them in the closest place in my life.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is God → self → others → tasks. The self-ruled treat their spouse as a tool for reaching their own goals, so tasks matter more than people; the self-emptied see their spouse as the “2” God has entrusted to them, so people matter more than tasks. Don’t let housework, money, or saving face hurt your most important “2.”
lessons.jesus: As soon as Jesus left the synagogue, he went into Simon’s house. Simon’s mother-in-law was lying sick with a fever, and Jesus “came and took her by the hand and raised her up” (Mark 1:31). After his public ministry before the crowds, Jesus brought healing into an ordinary home. Jesus shows us that his love is not only in the synagogue, but also behind the front door, with those closest to us.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for placing us in the closest place in each other’s lives. We confess that we often give our best to outsiders and save our worst for our family. Forgive us for the times we have bitten and devoured each other. Help us serve one another in love, and let our spouse truly become our most important “2” on earth. Amen.
teach: The 321 approach has a simple, memorable practice called 920 (my spouse is my most important “2”; practice the “0” of self-emptying; bear the “9”-fold fruit). Let’s spell it out this week: the “2” is every person I am in relationship with; the “0” is practicing the self-emptied life; the “9” is bearing the nine flavors of the fruit of the Spirit. The nine flavors aren’t developed alone on a mountaintop; they grow in relationships. Without the “2,” the “9” has nowhere to grow. And of all my “2”s, my spouse is my most important “2.”

Paul says, “through love be servants to one another. For the whole law is fulfilled in one word, in this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’” (Galatians 5:13–14). A “neighbor” is someone near me. Who is nearer than our spouse? We share the same bed, the same dinner table, the same bank account. We are often patient with outsiders and polite to colleagues, but when we come home, we save our worst side for the person closest to us.

Paul also gives a warning: “But if you bite and devour one another, be careful that you don’t consume one another” (Galatians 5:15). This is a very realistic picture of marriage: one cutting remark bites, another bites back, nobody wins, and both get hurt. The practice of 920 starts right here: putting our spouse back in the place of “my most important 2,” serving them in love instead of biting them with our words.
q: Of all my relationships, is my spouse truly my “most important 2”? Who most often gets my time, my patience, and my smiles?
Was there a recent time when my spouse and I “bit and devoured” each other? In that moment, what was I really trying to protect?
talk: When do you most feel that you are “the most important person to me”? When do you feel you’ve been put further down the list?
What small signal could we agree on to remind each other: “Stop, let’s not bite any more”?
acts: Tell your spouse today: “You’re the most important person to me.”
Put your phone down for ten minutes and give your full attention as your spouse tells you about their day
Write down three of your “2”s and pray one sentence for each
lessons.noon: “through love be servants to one another” — Lord, right now bring my spouse to mind, and help me serve them with one small action.

lessons.title: The “0” of Self-Emptying: A Grain of Wheat Falls
lessons.theme: Self-emptying is not losing yourself; it is bearing much fruit

v: Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.
He who loves his life will lose it. He who hates his life in this world will keep it to eternal life.
If anyone serves me, let him follow me. Where I am, there my servant will also be. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him.

lessons.still: Imagine holding a grain of wheat in your hand. The tighter you grip it, the more it stays just one grain. Slowly open your hand and tell the Lord: “Lord, I am willing to place the self I’ve been gripping so tightly into your hands.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The root of the problem is the self-ruled life: making ourselves the center, with self on the throne. We can’t get rid of self-rule by willpower; only through the gospel: Jesus’ death dealt with my sin and my old self, and Jesus’ resurrection gives me new life. So the “0” is not self-suppression; it is handing ourselves over to the Lord who died and rose again.
lessons.jesus: Right after speaking about the grain of wheat, Jesus said honestly, “Now my soul is troubled. What shall I say? ‘Father, save me from this time’? But I came to this time for this cause” (John 12:27). Jesus’ “0” didn’t mean having no feelings; in real struggle, he still chose the Father’s will. And because this grain of wheat fell into the ground, it bore the fruit of countless saved lives.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for falling into the earth for us and bearing the fruit of salvation. We confess that we often grip ourselves tightly, afraid of losing out. Through your death, put away our old selves; through your resurrection, give us new life. Help us practice self-emptying at home, not as resentful suppression, but as hopeful surrender. Amen.
teach: The “0” in 920 is practicing the self-emptied life. This “0” is often misunderstood as “I don’t matter” or “I have no voice.” But Jesus said, “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). When a grain falls into the ground, it isn’t destroyed; it enters another form of life. Self-emptied does not mean empty; it means entering the limitless and living out of the limitless.

Why must the “9” pass through the “0”? Because for the self-ruled, every fruit first has to answer: “What’s in it for me?” I give love in order to be loved; I’m patient to prove I’m the better person. Such fruit actually “remains by itself alone.” Jesus said, “He who loves his life will lose it” (John 12:25). If we cling to our rights, our pride, and being right, the marriage is left with two hard seeds, each intact, but with no harvest.

In marriage, “falling into the earth” is often very ordinary: being the first to make peace even when you’re in the right; getting up to help your spouse finish something when you’d rather rest; letting go of “I told you so.” These little deaths grow unexpected fruit in the home: trust, warmth, laughter. The “0” is not the end; it is where the “9” begins.
q: In our marriage, what am I gripping most tightly and refusing to let “fall into the earth”? Pride, being right, my time, or some right of mine?
When I hear “self-emptied,” is my first reaction fear of loss or hope of fruit? Why?
talk: Think back to a time when you set yourself aside for me. What fruit did that later bear in our home?
This week, is there a small thing where we are both willing to “fall into the earth” first and stop insisting on our own way?
acts: In one small thing today, let go of “I’m right”
Tell your spouse: “Let’s do it your way this time.”
Write down one “tightly held thing” you are willing to hand over to the Lord
lessons.noon: “But if it dies, it bears much fruit” — Lord, right now I let go of insisting, and ask you to make my home bear fruit.

lessons.title: Love: Walking in Love
lessons.theme: Love is not a trade; it gives itself up, as Christ did

v: Be therefore imitators of God, as beloved children.
Walk in love, even as Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling fragrance.

lessons.still: Picture a child watching their father work, then picking up a tool to copy him. Quietly tell the Lord: “Father, I am your beloved child. Today I want to learn from you how to love my spouse.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Self-ruled love is a trade: “If you treat me well, I’ll treat you well.” Pride provokes pride, and love as a trade ends up as mutual scorekeeping. Self-emptied love is an overflow: because God has already loved me enough, I can love first. Humility inspires humility, and the one who loves first often draws out love from the other.
lessons.jesus: Judas came with a crowd to arrest Jesus, using a kiss as the signal. Jesus said to him, “Friend, why are you here?” (Matthew 26:50). Facing the one who betrayed him, Jesus still called him “friend.” Jesus is our example: love doesn’t depend on whether the other person deserves it, because the source of love is in the Father.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving us while we were still sinners and making us your beloved children. Our love often runs dry and often keeps score. Help us imitate you and walk in love, giving ourselves up for our spouse as Christ did, no longer loving as a trade, but loving first and loving always. Amen.
teach: The first of the nine flavors is love. A Greek word often used in the New Testament, agape, does not mean love drawn out by attraction, nor love as a trade, but the kind of love God has: love that gives itself freely, whether or not the other person deserves it. Marriage needs romance and friendship too, but when the tide of romance goes out and friendship grows weary, it is this love that comes from God that holds a home together.

Paul says, “Be therefore imitators of God, as beloved children” (Ephesians 5:1). Children learn from their parents not by memorizing rules, but by watching and copying every day. Love is learned the same way: first knowing that we are God’s deeply loved children, and then learning to love the way our heavenly Father loves. Someone unsure of being loved often loves with strings attached; only someone sure of being loved can give freely.

This is what that love looks like: “Walk in love, even as Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us” (Ephesians 5:2). Paul says elsewhere, “while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). God didn’t wait for us to improve before loving us. At home, love means treating our spouse well before they have changed, and choosing to love them even on a day when they are not lovable. Before God, such love is “a sweet-smelling fragrance” (Ephesians 5:2).
q: Lately, has my love for my spouse looked more like a “trade” or an “overflow” of what God has poured in? How can I tell?
When I feel my love running dry, what do I usually do? Do I go back to God first?
talk: Was there a time when you kept loving me even when I was “unlovable”? How did that affect me? (Let the one who was loved speak first and give thanks.)
This week, what specific way would you most like me to show you my love?
acts: Today, do something for your spouse without being asked
Spend five quiet minutes simply thanking God for his love for you
Let go of one “I’ll change when they change first” thought
lessons.noon: “Walk in love, even as Christ also loved us” — Father, right now let me learn from you and love first.

lessons.title: What Love Looks Like at Home
lessons.theme: Love is not only in words but in deed and truth

v: By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.
But whoever has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, then closes his heart of compassion against him, how does God’s love remain in him?
My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.
A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.
By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

lessons.still: Think back over every small thing you’ve done at home since this morning: a glass of water, a greeting, a glance. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, in these small things, where was your love? Where was it missing?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: When life changes, daily living changes. If love stays only in our ideas, it hasn’t yet become life; if it stays only in our feelings, it hasn’t yet entered daily living. The practice of 920 has to take root in the small things of every day: life first, then relationship. Change begins with me, not with “waiting for my spouse to change.”
lessons.jesus: After his resurrection, Jesus made a charcoal fire on the shore, cooked fish and bread, and said to his tired disciples, “Come and eat breakfast!” (John 21:12). The risen Lord didn’t start with a sermon; he started by preparing breakfast. Jesus shows us that the deepest love is often hidden in the most everyday care.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for laying down your life for us, so that we know what love is. Help us love not only with our lips, but in deed and truth. Let my spouse be my most important “2,” let me practice self-emptying in you, and let the Holy Spirit bear abundant fruit in our home, so that all who see our family recognize you. Amen.
teach: John says, “let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth” (1 John 3:18). Many couples say “I love you” easily, yet rarely ask: what does my love actually look like? Love at home is usually not some dramatic sacrifice. It is a glass of warm water, a pair of socks washed and put away, a “Thanks for all your hard work today,” and after an argument, being the first to climb down.

John first names the source of love: “By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us” (1 John 3:16). Love is defined not by my feelings but by the cross. Jesus also said, “Just as I have loved you, you also love one another” (John 13:34). “Just as” is key: not in the way I’m used to, but in the way Jesus loves me, I love my most important “2.”

This week we have seen the whole picture of 920: my spouse is my most important “2,” I practice the “0” of self-emptying, and I let the Holy Spirit bear the “9” flavors of fruit. Love is the first flavor, and the root of the other eight, nourishing the whole tree like a root system. Over the next eight weeks, we’ll taste one flavor each week. There is no need to rush for it all to grow at once. Fruit needs seasons, and we’ll grow slowly together.
q: If my love for my spouse this week were filmed, what “deeds” would the video show? Or would it be mostly “words”?
Of the 2, 0, and 9 in 920, which number do I most need to practice right now?
talk: For you, what small things make you feel most “loved”? Please give one or two specific examples.
Looking back over this week, what is the one sentence each of us most wants to carry into next week? (If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down what you’d like to say to them.)
acts: Today, do a household task your spouse often does but is rarely thanked for
Thank your spouse specifically, naming what they did
On your 920 tree, write one thing you want to practice next week
lessons.noon: “let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth” — Lord, right now let me show my spouse love with one action.

14.title: The Fruit of the Spirit (2): Joy

mem.t: Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!”

s: Together, find an empty can or glass jar and decorate it as “our family’s thank-you jar.”
Each write five little notes, each naming one small thing your spouse did this week that brought you joy. Fold them up and put them in the jar.
Take turns drawing out a note and reading it aloud. The person being thanked simply replies: “Thank you for noticing.”
Read Philippians 4:4 together, and agree to add a few notes to the jar every week from now on.

lessons.title: Rejoice in the Lord Always
lessons.theme: The source of joy is not our circumstances but the Lord himself

v: Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!”
Let your gentleness be known to all men. The Lord is at hand.
In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

lessons.still: Take a deep breath, then slowly let it out. Set down the things weighing on you today, one by one, and tell the Lord: “Lord, my joy doesn’t depend on things going well; it is found in you.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keep the focus on Jesus, not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances. Pinning our joy on our spouse is asking them to play God’s role, an unfair burden for them to carry. Let people be people, and let God be God: when my joy comes from the Lord, my spouse is set free from “the job of making me happy.”
lessons.jesus: On the night he was betrayed, Jesus prayed to the Father, “But now I come to you, and I say these things in the world, that they may have my joy made full in themselves” (John 17:13). The cross was right before him, yet he wanted to share his own joy with his disciples. Jesus shows us that joy wells up from our relationship with the Father, and he gladly gives that joy to us.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for being the source of our joy. We confess that we often let our circumstances and each other’s behavior decide our mood. Today we hand all our worries to you. Give us the joy that comes from you, so that we stop demanding that each other fill us, and instead rejoice together in you. Amen.
teach: When Paul wrote Philippians, he was in prison with an uncertain future. Yet in this short letter, words about joy appear again and again. He says, “Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, ‘Rejoice!’” (Philippians 4:4). He says it twice, as if he knows his readers will wonder: “Can anyone really rejoice in a situation like this?” Paul’s answer is yes, because this joy is “in the Lord.”

Happiness and joy are not the same. Happiness is like the weather, changing with circumstances: we’re happy when we get a raise, unhappy when the kids won’t listen, and unhappy all day when our spouse forgets our anniversary. Joy is more like the deep ocean: the surface can be whipped up by wind and waves, yet the depths remain calm. The joy the Spirit produces is knowing that the Lord is with me and in control of everything, so my heart holds a steadiness and gladness that can’t be taken away.

Paul also shows us how to enter into this joy: “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God” (Philippians 4:6). What most often steals a couple’s joy is not some great disaster, but accumulated worries: bills, work, children, parents. When we bring our worries to God together, joy has room to grow.
q: Lately, has my joy been more like the “weather” or the “deep ocean”? What changes my mood most easily?
Have I, without realizing it, placed the responsibility of “making me happy” on my spouse?
talk: What worries have been weighing on your heart lately? How can we hand them to God together today?
When do you think our home feels most joyful? What are we usually doing at those times?
acts: Write down one worry today, and pray it over with your spouse, entrusting it to God
Tell your spouse: “You don’t have to be responsible for making me happy. I’m doing well in the Lord.”
Find a moment today to quietly recite Philippians 4:4
lessons.noon: “Rejoice in the Lord always” — Lord, right now, whatever my situation, I choose to rejoice in you.

lessons.title: Even Though the Vines Bear No Fruit
lessons.theme: Joy doesn’t depend on the harvest, but on the God who saves me

v: For even though the fig tree doesn’t flourish, nor fruit be in the vines, the labor of the olive fails, the fields yield no food, the flocks are cut off from the fold, and there is no herd in the stalls,
yet I will rejoice in the LORD. I will be joyful in the God of my salvation!
GOD, the Lord, is my strength. He makes my feet like deer’s feet, and enables me to go in high places. For the music director, on my stringed instruments.

lessons.still: Picture a parched field: no fruit on the trees, no sheep in the fold. In the middle of that field, someone lifts their head and sings. Quietly ask yourself: “Where in my field is there still no harvest?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: From a human point of view, no harvest means no reason for joy; from God’s point of view, God himself is the reason. As we turn from earth to heaven and from the temporary to the eternal, joy is no longer tied to the harvest. This isn’t passive resignation; it is actively letting Jesus reign.
lessons.jesus: After the Last Supper, “When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives” (Matthew 26:30). Gethsemane and the cross lay just ahead, yet he sang with his disciples. Jesus’ joy did not depend on his circumstances; it was built on trust in the Father’s will.
lessons.pray: God who saves us, you see the trees in our home that have not yet borne fruit, and you see the disappointment in our hearts. We won’t pretend it doesn’t hurt, but we choose to look to you. Be our strength, steady our feet on the high places, and after every “even though,” help us say “yet” together. Amen.
teach: The prophet Habakkuk wrote one of the bravest songs in the Bible: “For even though the fig tree doesn’t flourish, nor fruit be in the vines... yet I will rejoice in the LORD. I will be joyful in the God of my salvation!” (Habakkuk 3:17–18). In an agricultural society, these words amount to saying: my paycheck is gone, my savings are gone, every security I had is gone. And after all those “even though”s, he speaks one “yet.”

Every couple goes through seasons when “the vines bear no fruit”: perhaps long-term financial pressure, perhaps a child longed for who still hasn’t come, perhaps a parent’s illness, a setback at work, or a low point in the marriage itself. The Bible doesn’t ask us to pretend these don’t hurt. Habakkuk’s joy is not denial of reality; it is choosing, after seeing reality clearly, to turn our eyes to God anyway.

His reason is this: “GOD, the Lord, is my strength. He makes my feet like deer’s feet, and enables me to go in high places” (Habakkuk 3:19). A deer on a steep mountain path doesn’t rely on the path being smooth, but on the sureness of its feet. Joy doesn’t flatten the mountain path, but it does steady our feet. When a husband and wife say “yet” together in hard times, they are helping each other stand firm.
q: What “vine” in our home still bears no fruit? What do I honestly feel about it deep down?
After that “even though,” can I honestly speak a “yet” to God?
talk: What is the biggest “even though” in our home right now? Let’s finish this sentence together: “Even though…, yet we will rejoice in God, because…”
In hard seasons, how would you most like me to be with you, instead of rushing to cheer you up?
acts: Write your family’s own “Even though… yet…” sentence
Today, don’t rush to comfort your spouse; first listen until they’ve said everything on their heart
Set Habakkuk 3:18 as your phone wallpaper
lessons.noon: “yet I will rejoice in the LORD. I will be joyful in the God of my salvation!” — Lord, right now, even when things aren’t going my way, I still rejoice in you.

lessons.title: A Home That Gives Thanks in Everything
lessons.theme: Thanksgiving is the soil of joy and the culture of a home

v: Always rejoice.
Pray without ceasing.
In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.
Praise the LORD, my soul! All that is within me, praise his holy name!
Praise the LORD, my soul, and don’t forget all his benefits,

lessons.still: Be still for a moment and count three small things from today that you’re thankful for, plus one more that has to do with your spouse. Slowly tell the Lord: “Lord, thank you. All of these are your gifts.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Complaining is the language of the self-ruled life, because the focus is on “what I didn’t get”; thanksgiving is the language of the self-emptied life, because the focus is on “what God has already given.” Change your mindset and your life will change: when I shift from “they should have done it” to “thank you for doing it,” the air in our home changes.
lessons.jesus: At Lazarus’ tomb, before the dead man had come out, Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, “Father, I thank you that you listened to me” (John 11:41). He gave thanks before he saw the result. Jesus shows us that thanksgiving isn’t something we say only once everything is fine; in trust, we speak it first.
lessons.pray: Gracious Lord, we often forget your benefits, and we often take our spouse’s efforts for granted. Open our eyes to see your grace every day. Help us say more thanks and fewer complaints at home, so that thanksgiving becomes our family’s culture and joy becomes the air in our home. Amen.
teach: Paul puts three things together: “Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks” (1 Thessalonians 5:16–18). Joy, prayer, and thanksgiving are like three strands woven together. Thanksgiving is especially like soil: the same seed won’t grow in hard ground, but sprouts in soft, loose earth. In a home where people often say “thank you,” joy grows easily.

David tells himself, “Praise the LORD, my soul, and don’t forget all his benefits” (Psalm 103:2). He has to remind himself, because people forget so easily. Marriage is the same: when we were newly married, we were touched when our spouse poured us a glass of water; ten years later, they pour us water every day and we take it for granted. Taking things for granted is the biggest thief of gratitude.

Thanksgiving can become a family culture. Culture isn’t built by one moving moment, but by repeated habits: a prayer of thanks before meals, naming one thing you’re thankful for in your spouse before bed, and saying it out loud, specifically, when a child or family member does something good. Notice that Paul says “In everything give thanks,” not “give thanks for everything.” We don’t give thanks for bad things, but in anything at all, we can still find God’s grace.
q: Of the things my spouse does for me, which one have I long taken for granted and not said thank you for in a long time?
In the words I’ve spoken lately, have there been more complaints or more thanks?
talk: Each name three things from this week you want to thank the other for. The more specific, the better.
What small habit of thanksgiving could our family build, so that it happens every day or every week?
acts: Say a specific “Thank you for…” to your spouse three times today
When you pray before a meal, add a sentence thanking God for your spouse
Before bed, each share the one thing you are most thankful for today
lessons.noon: “In everything give thanks” — Lord, right now I give you thanks for one small thing.

lessons.title: Bringing Joy Home
lessons.theme: The joy of the Lord is the strength of the whole family

v: Then he said to them, “Go your way. Eat the fat, drink the sweet, and send portions to him for whom nothing is prepared, for today is holy to our Lord. Don’t be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.”
A glad heart makes a cheerful face, but an aching heart breaks the spirit.
All the days of the afflicted are wretched, but one who has a cheerful heart enjoys a continual feast.

lessons.still: Think about the moment you arrive at your front door each day. What expression do you carry in with you? Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, today let me bring your joy through the door, not my exhaustion.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Live from the heart and you find joy; live from the head and you fret. Come home with a head full of work and calculations, and home becomes just another office; hand your heart to the Holy Spirit, and joy will flow out. People matter more than tasks: don’t let the day’s tasks crush the people in your home.
lessons.jesus: Passing through Jericho, Jesus looked up at Zacchaeus in the tree and said, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house,” and Zacchaeus “hurried, came down, and received him joyfully” (Luke 19:5–6). When Jesus walked into that home, it was filled with joy and change. When we let Jesus into our own hearts first, we will carry his joy home with us.
lessons.pray: Lord, forgive us for so often bringing our bad moods home and making the people closest to us bear our exhaustion. Let the joy of the Lord be our strength, so that we walk through the door with smiles and blessings, and our home becomes good medicine for each other rather than another battlefield. Amen.
teach: Proverbs says, “A glad heart makes a cheerful face, but an aching heart breaks the spirit” (Proverbs 15:13). The atmosphere in a home is a lot like air conditioning: when one person walks in angry, the whole house cools down. Many people are all smiles with clients at work, but at home they dump all their exhaustion and bad moods on the people closest to them. We give our best to strangers and save our worst for our family.

Joy flows from the heart to the face. This isn’t a call to put on a fake smile; it’s a reminder that one person’s heart affects the whole dinner table. Proverbs also says, “one who has a cheerful heart enjoys a continual feast” (Proverbs 15:15). The same plain rice and vegetables are a feast to a joyful heart; the finest delicacies taste of nothing to a bitter one.

When the people heard God’s law and remembered their failures, they wept. But Nehemiah told them, “Don’t be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength” (Nehemiah 8:10). Joy is not just a mood; it is strength. Couples can practice a “doorway prayer”: with your hand on the doorknob, take a breath, say one sentence to the Lord, and then open the door and walk in. Those few seconds can turn the day’s battlefield into the rest of home.
q: Looking back over this week, what expression and mood did I most often carry through the front door?
Have I, without realizing it, been taking out the pressures of the outside world on my spouse?
talk: When I get home each day (or when you do), how would you like us to greet each other?
What small things best help you laugh again after an exhausting day?
acts: Before you open the door when you get home today, pray a “doorway prayer”
As soon as you walk in, give your spouse a smile or a hug before saying anything else
At dinner, share one thing that made you laugh today
lessons.noon: “the joy of the LORD is your strength” — Lord, right now renew my heart, and let me bring joy home.

lessons.title: A Couple Who Weep and Rejoice Together
lessons.theme: True joy is not never crying, but walking together until morning comes

v: For his anger is but for a moment. His favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning.
You have turned my mourning into dancing for me. You have removed my sackcloth, and clothed me with gladness,
to the end that my heart may sing praise to you, and not be silent. LORD my God, I will give thanks to you forever!
Therefore you now have sorrow, but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy away from you.

lessons.still: Be still and consider what has been going on in your spouse’s heart lately: are they rejoicing, or are they grieving? Tell the Lord: “Lord, help my heart keep pace with theirs.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled only want others to match their own emotions: when I’m happy, you should laugh with me; when I’m sad, you should understand me. The self-emptied first set aside their own channel and tune in to their spouse’s. When two are of one heart, joy is doubled and sorrow is halved. This is the beauty of God’s design in making husband and wife one.
lessons.jesus: Jesus knew he was about to raise Lazarus, yet when he saw Mary weeping, “he groaned in the spirit and was troubled” (John 11:33), and “Jesus wept” (John 11:35). He didn’t rush to say, “Don’t cry, it’ll be fine in a minute.” Jesus is our example: first weep with those who weep, then bring the joy of resurrection.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for being with us in our nights of weeping, and for promising that joy comes in the morning. Give us soft hearts, able to rejoice with our spouse without envy, and to weep with our spouse without impatience. Turn our family’s mourning into dancing, so that our hearts sing praise to you forever. Amen.
teach: Picture a couple: on the day the husband is promoted, the wife feels a twinge of envy; on another day, when the wife is sad, the husband rushes to say, “Don’t overthink it.” Rejoicing together requires self-emptying, not envy; weeping together also requires self-emptying, not rushing to fix the other’s feelings. Since husband and wife are one, when one rejoices, the other rejoices too; when one suffers, the other shares the load.

The fruit of joy doesn’t mean we must smile all the time. The psalmist says, “Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning” (Psalm 30:5). Scripture admits there is weeping in the night; it only promises the night won’t last forever. The nights a couple walks through together might be a job loss, a miscarriage, the long wait of infertility, the death of a loved one, or a crisis in the marriage. Godly joy doesn’t skip these nights; it holds hands through the night and waits for morning together.

Jesus told his grieving disciples, “you now have sorrow, but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy away from you” (John 16:22). This week we have seen that the source of joy is the Lord; that joy doesn’t depend on the harvest; that thanksgiving is the soil of joy; that joy can be brought home; and that joy at its deepest is two people weeping and rejoicing together in the Lord. Next week we’ll taste the third flavor: peace.
q: When my spouse has good news, can I truly rejoice for them? Or is there comparison or envy in my heart?
When my spouse is sad, do I more often weep with them, or rush to give answers and want them to feel better quickly?
talk: Think back to a “night” we walked through together. What made you feel you weren’t alone then?
Of this week’s practices of joy, which habit would you most like us to keep?
acts: Ask your spouse today: “Lately, does your heart feel more like weeping or laughing?”
Celebrate a recent good thing in your spouse’s life in a specific way
Read Psalm 30:5 together, and pray for friends or family going through a dark night
lessons.noon: “Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning” — Lord, right now I hand you my tears in the night, and I wait for your morning.

mem.t: And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body, and be thankful.

date.t: An Evening of Tearing Down a Wall
s: Get a few building blocks or sticky notes. Each of you writes down one thing that has recently “put up a little wall” between you (start with “I,” and don’t write accusations).
Take turns sharing. The one listening responds only with: “Thank you for telling me. I hear you.”
Together, knock the blocks over or tear up the notes, and say: “Christ has broken down the middle wall of separation.”
Holding hands, read Colossians 3:15 aloud and ask that the peace Christ gives would rule in our hearts.

lessons.title: Let Christ’s Peace Rule
lessons.theme: Peace in the home begins with who is ruling in our hearts

v: Above all these things, walk in love, which is the bond of perfection.
And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body, and be thankful.
Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, I give to you. Don’t let your heart be troubled, neither let it be fearful.

lessons.still: Place your hand on your chest and feel your heartbeat. Quietly ask: “Right now, what is ruling my heart: anxiety, anger, or the peace of Christ?” Then say to the Lord: “Lord, please take the throne of my heart.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: A home often lacks peace because it has two kings: I want to be in charge, and so do you. Pride against pride, and both lose. When we let Jesus reign, husband and wife both return to our rightful place, and peace has a foundation. Whoever rules in the heart rules in the home.
lessons.jesus: When the storm raged, Jesus was in the stern, “asleep on the cushion” (Mark 4:38). He woke and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” (Mark 4:39). His calm did not come from the absence of wind and waves, but from complete trust in the Father. Jesus had peace within first, and that brought calm without.
lessons.pray: Lord of peace, thank you for leaving us your peace. We confess that we often let anger, anxiety, and our own opinions rule our hearts. Today we hand the throne of our hearts back to you. Let your peace be the umpire within us, so that as husband and wife we stop fighting over who is in charge and instead submit to you together. Amen.
teach: Paul writes, “let the peace of God rule in your hearts” (Colossians 3:15). The word translated “rule” originally meant “to act as umpire,” like a referee on the field who blows the final whistle. When two voices argue inside us—“I’m going to snap back” and “I’m going to stay quiet”—who blows the whistle? Paul says: let God’s peace, the peace Christ gives, be the referee.

This peace is different from what the world gives. Jesus said, “My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, I give to you” (John 14:27). The world’s peace is conditional: I’ll have peace once the problem is solved, once my spouse apologizes. Christ’s peace is relational: because he is with me, even before the problem is solved there is already an unshakable center in my heart. Peace in the home has to begin with peace in each heart.

Just before this, Paul says, “Above all these things, walk in love, which is the bond of perfection” (Colossians 3:14). Last week’s love and joy and this week’s peace are really one fruit. He also says we “were called in one body.” A husband and wife are called to become one—not to fight over who is in charge, but together to let Jesus reign.
q: Lately, when my spouse and I disagree, what usually “blows the whistle” in my heart: anger, fear, or the peace of Christ?
Does my peace usually have to wait until my spouse changes first or apologizes first?
talk: When do you feel our home has the most peace? When is it most tense?
When peace starts to slip away in our hearts, what short phrase could we use to remind each other to “let Christ’s peace rule”?
acts: Today, when emotions rise, pause for three seconds and pray silently: “Lord, you rule.”
Tell your spouse: “Today I want to let Christ’s peace rule.”
Before bed, read John 14:27 together
lessons.noon: “let the peace of God rule in your hearts” — Lord, right now let your peace blow the whistle and rule in my heart.

lessons.title: Breaking Down the Dividing Wall
lessons.theme: The wall the cross tore down—let’s not build it back up

v: For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation,
having abolished in his flesh the hostility, the law of commandments contained in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man of the two, making peace,
and might reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, having killed the hostility through it.
He came and preached peace to you who were far off and to those who were near.

lessons.still: Picture a brick wall standing between you and your spouse, each brick inscribed with something never talked through. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, you know which bricks are between us. Help us take them down one by one.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The wall is actually built from the self-ruled life: my grievances, my pride, my being right. Every brick is there to protect me. Only the self-emptied can become one: when I’m willing to remove the bricks on my side first, the wall starts to shrink. Change starts with me, not with the other person.
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was arrested, the disciples scattered, and Peter denied him three times. Yet the risen Jesus “himself stood among them, and said to them, ‘Peace be to you’” (Luke 24:36). He didn’t settle accounts first; he tore down the wall first. Jesus shows us that the first step toward reconciliation is often taken by the one who was hurt.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for tearing down the wall between us and God on the cross, and for making us as husband and wife one. Wherever walls have quietly gone up between us, give us courage to take them down together. Let us stop protecting our pride and start protecting our oneness. Amen.
teach: Paul says Jesus “is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation” (Ephesians 2:14). In the temple of that day there really was a wall that kept Gentiles out. The hostility between Jews and Gentiles ran deeper than any conflict between spouses today, yet the cross made these two groups into “one new man” (Ephesians 2:15). If Christ could tear down a wall that thick, the walls in our home can come down too.

The wall between a husband and wife usually isn’t built in a day. An argument with no apology, a need that was overlooked, a disappointment never voiced—each one is a brick. Over time, two people live under the same roof yet seem to live on opposite sides of a wall. Cold silences, each scrolling our own phone, talking only about the kids and the bills—these are signs the wall has grown high.

Paul says Christ came to “reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, having killed the hostility through it” (Ephesians 2:16). The foundation of peace is not which of us communicates better, but that we have both been reconciled to God. When I remember how God tore down the wall between himself and me, I become more willing to remove my brick first. Peace doesn’t mean waiting for the wall to fall on its own; it means taking it down together.
q: Is there a “brick” between my spouse and me that hasn’t been removed yet? What is written on it?
Am I waiting for my spouse to tear down the wall first, or am I willing to start? What makes me hesitate?
talk: Do you sense a small wall that has slowly gone up between us lately? How could we take down the first brick together?
When there’s distance between us, how would you most like me to come close to you?
acts: Today, gently bring up a small matter you’ve never talked through
At dinner tonight, put your phones in another room
Apologize to your spouse for a “little wall” you once put up
lessons.noon: “broke down the middle wall of separation” — Lord, right now I am willing to remove the bricks on my side first.

lessons.title: True Peace, Not False Peace
lessons.theme: Peace is not the absence of conflict but the ability to reconcile

v: They have healed also the hurt of my people superficially, saying, ‘Peace, peace!’ when there is no peace.
Better is a dry morsel with quietness, than a house full of feasting with strife.
For lack of wood a fire goes out. Without gossip, a quarrel dies down.

lessons.still: Ask yourself honestly: “In our home, is there something we deliberately avoid mentioning, as if it doesn’t exist?” Quietly place it before the Lord. You don’t need to rush to fix it—just admit that it’s there.
lessons.light: 321 Light: False peace is often the self-ruled life in another form: fear of conflict is really fear of being hurt or losing face. True peace takes humility: willingness to speak the truth and willingness to hear it. Proverbs says, “Better is a dry morsel with quietness, than a house full of feasting with strife” (Proverbs 17:1), because people matter more than issues.
lessons.jesus: Jesus taught, “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone” (Matthew 18:15). Jesus didn’t tell us to pretend nothing happened. He told us to deal with it privately, directly, and with a heart to restore—so that “you have gained back your brother,” not so that you win the argument.
lessons.pray: Righteous and loving Lord, we don’t want false peace; we want your true peace. Give us courage to speak the truth and humility to hear it. Heal with your own hand every wound that has been covered up in our home. If anyone is in danger, protect them, open a way, and lead them to help. Amen.
teach: God rebuked the leaders of that day: “They have healed also the hurt of my people superficially, saying, ‘Peace, peace!’ when there is no peace” (Jeremiah 6:14). Some homes are very quiet, but they are not at peace. Problems get swept under the rug, everyone pretends all is well, and the wounds fester underneath. The peace the Spirit produces does not pretend there is no conflict; it has the power to face conflict and move toward reconciliation.

Proverbs reminds us of the other side: “For lack of wood a fire goes out. Without gossip, a quarrel dies down” (Proverbs 26:20). Conflict is like a fire, and some words are firewood: digging up the past, sarcasm, complaining about your spouse to others. People of peace don’t run from problems; they stop adding fuel and deal with the fire while it’s still small: “What I just said was too harsh. Can we start over?”

One more thing must be said clearly: peace is never bought at the cost of safety. If there is physical, verbal, sexual, or financial abuse and control in the home, keeping silent to “keep the peace” is not biblical peace—it is the false peace Jeremiah described. In that case, safety comes first; seek help from a pastor and from professionals. The peace God wants is true, just, and safe.
q: How do I usually handle conflict: pretend nothing’s wrong, blow up, or talk it through gently?
Is there something I keep brushing off—“Forget it, it’s fine”—while my heart still hurts?
talk: When something unpleasant comes up between us, would you rather we talk right away, or cool down first? How soon should we talk?
Could we agree on a phrase that lets each other know, “I want to talk, not fight”?
acts: Today, clear up a small misunderstanding while the fire is still small
Write down one thing you want to talk about with your spouse but have been avoiding
Note down the contact details of your church’s pastor or a counseling resource
lessons.noon: “Better is a dry morsel with quietness” — Lord, right now help me value peace in my family more than being right.

lessons.title: Be a Peacemaker
lessons.theme: Peacemakers are willing to yield first

v: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.
There was strife between the herdsmen of Abram’s livestock and the herdsmen of Lot’s livestock. The Canaanites and the Perizzites lived in the land at that time.
Abram said to Lot, “Please, let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen; for we are relatives.
Isn’t the whole land before you? Please separate yourself from me. If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right. Or if you go to the right hand, then I will go to the left.”

lessons.still: Picture two paths forking in front of you. You stop and let the other person choose first. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, today at home, I want to be the one who yields first.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride provokes pride—one hard word draws back a harder one; humility draws out humility—one soft word often softens the other person too. A peacemaker is someone who first becomes the “0,” self-emptied, not needing to win, seeking only oneness. This is the path where husband and wife both win.
lessons.jesus: When the disciples argued on the road about who was the greatest, Jesus, back in the house, didn’t let the argument go on. He sat down and said, “If any man wants to be first, he shall be last of all, and servant of all” (Mark 9:35). Jesus dealt with conflict at its root: turning a heart that grasps for greatness into a heart that serves.
lessons.pray: Lord, you are the God of peace, and you call us to be peacemakers. Forgive us for the times we’ve poured fuel on the fire and the times we refused to give an inch. Give us Abram’s largeness of heart, valuing family ties above our own rights, so that between husband and wife, parents and children, and with our in-laws, we become people who yield first and bring peace. Amen.
teach: Jesus said, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). Notice: not “peace-lovers” but “peacemakers.” The first simply don’t want to fight; the second actively bring about reconciliation. God himself is the God who makes peace, so peacemakers look most like his children.

When Abram’s and Lot’s herdsmen quarreled, Abram said to Lot, “Please, let there be no strife between you and me... for we are relatives” (Genesis 13:8). He valued the relationship above the pastureland, even letting the younger Lot choose first: “If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right. Or if you go to the right hand, then I will go to the left” (Genesis 13:9). As the elder, he could have chosen first, but he chose to yield. Peacemakers are often those willing to lay down their rights first.

Being a peacemaker at home isn’t only about handling conflict between husband and wife. It also means being the one who cools things down—not the one who pours fuel on the fire—among children, parents, and in-laws. Peace is not the result of one big negotiation but of daily choices: a gentle tone, listening all the way through before responding, a decision not to dig up the past, a simple “You choose first this time.”
q: In conflicts at home, am I more often the one who cools things down, or the one who adds fuel?
At home, is there something where I keep insisting, “I choose first; what I say goes”?
talk: Think back to a time we made up after a fight. What word or action turned the atmosphere around?
In our families of origin or with our in-laws, is there a place where we need to be peacemakers together?
acts: Today, in a small moment of friction, respond first with a gentle tone
Pray for a family member with whom things are tense, asking God for peace
Say something to your spouse that cools things down: “No rush—let’s take it slowly.”
lessons.noon: “let there be no strife between you and me” — Lord, right now help me value the relationship more than winning the argument.

lessons.title: Peace Be to This House
lessons.theme: Pursue peace, build one another up, and make home a house of peace

v: for God’s Kingdom is not eating and drinking, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.
For he who serves Christ in these things is acceptable to God and approved by men.
So then, let’s follow after things which make for peace, and things by which we may build one another up.
You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you.

lessons.still: Quietly look around your home: the living room, the dining table, the bedroom. In your heart, bless each corner: “Peace be to this house.” Finally, hold your spouse in your heart and say, “Lord, may your peace rest on him (her).”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Peace is not an outward arrangement but an inner life. It flows from the inside out: first Christ’s peace rules in my heart, then there is harmony in our marriage, and then our home can become a blessing to others. Life first, then relationships, then ministry—a home of peace is a small gospel outpost.
lessons.jesus: When Jesus sent out his disciples, he told them, “Into whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house’” (Luke 10:5). Jesus made his disciples people who carry peace into other people’s homes. When our own home has first received peace, we can bring that peace into others’ homes too.
lessons.pray: God of peace, thank you for leading us to learn about peace this week. Guard our hearts and make our minds steadfast in trusting you. Help us pursue what makes for peace and what builds one another up, so that our home becomes a house of peace and a blessing to others. Peace be to this house. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
teach: Paul says, “God’s Kingdom is not eating and drinking, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14:17). This verse ties together what we’ve learned these three weeks: love leads us to treat each other rightly, and peace and joy are both the work of the Spirit. When a home has these three, God’s Kingdom shows itself in that home.

Paul goes on: “let’s follow after things which make for peace, and things by which we may build one another up” (Romans 14:19). “Follow after” is an active verb, like a hunter on the trail of its prey. Peace doesn’t just fall into a home; it has to be pursued. In practice, that means asking with every choice: Is this word, this decision, tearing us down or building us up?

Isaiah says, “You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you” (Isaiah 26:3). The ultimate foundation of peace is not that both spouses are mature, but that both lean on God. This week we have seen how to let Christ’s peace rule, tear down the dividing wall, refuse false peace, be peacemakers, and pursue peace together. Next week we taste the fourth flavor of the fruit: patience.
q: Lately, have my words and decisions mostly been tearing down or building up our home?
Is my peace built on “everything is under control,” or on a mind that steadfastly trusts God?
talk: Through this week’s practice of peace, where do you think our home has changed, even a little?
Which family (relatives, friends, or neighbors) could we pray for together, asking God to give them peace?
acts: Today, say something to your spouse that builds them up
Pray for a family you know: “Peace be to this house.”
Before bed, read Isaiah 26:3 together
lessons.noon: “You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace” — Lord, right now I lean on you. Keep our home in perfect peace.

mem.t: with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love,

s: Go together to buy a packet of seeds or a small seedling—pick a plant you both like.
Plant it in a pot together and stick a small card on the pot: “Leave it this year also—we’ll wait together.”
Each of you name one way you’ve seen the other slowly grow over the past few years, and thank them for their effort.
Agree to care for this plant together over the coming weeks, reminding each other: growth takes time.

lessons.title: Bearing with One Another in Love
lessons.theme: Patience begins with humility and bears with one another in love

v: I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called,
with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love,
being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

lessons.still: Think of the little habit of your spouse’s that makes you sigh most often. Don’t rush to criticize. Simply place it before the Lord alongside one of your own little faults, and say: “Lord, we both need you to bear with us.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Impatience often comes from making myself the standard and expecting my spouse to live at my pace—that is the pride of the self-ruled life. Humility means returning to our rightful place: I am not my spouse’s lord; the Lord is. When I let people be people, and let God be God, I can bear with my spouse instead of trying to remake them.
lessons.jesus: When the disciples couldn’t drive out a demon and the crowd was arguing, Jesus said, “How long shall I bear with you? Bring him to me” (Mark 9:19). Jesus really did sigh, but his sigh didn’t turn into giving up; it turned into action: “Bring him to me.” This is Jesus’ long-fused love.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for always bearing with us. We confess that we often make ourselves the standard and lack patience with our spouse. Give us hearts of humility, gentleness, and patience, so that we bear with one another in love and eagerly keep the unity you have given, never letting small things tear down our home. Amen.
teach: Paul writes, “with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love” (Ephesians 4:2). These words are like a ring of keys, and the first key is humility. Why does patience begin with humility? Because what we find hardest to bear is often not another person’s wrongdoing, but that they “didn’t do it my way.” When I see that others need to be patient with me too, I find it easier to be patient with them.

The Greek word for patience is made of two parts, “long” and “temper”: a long fuse, slow to flare up. “Bearing with” means carrying, shouldering a load. Many things in marriage are not sins, just differences: how you squeeze the toothpaste, how fast you get out the door, the pace of your conversation. The best way to handle these is not to keep correcting, but to bear with them in love, like picking up a light piece of luggage.

Paul goes on: “being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:3). Unity is something the Spirit has already given; our job is to be eager to keep it. Patience is one way we keep that unity: we don’t let a small habit tear down a great marriage. A longer fuse makes for a roomier home.
q: The thing about my spouse that makes me most impatient—is it sin, or is it just “different from me”?
In what ways has my spouse been quietly bearing with me?
talk: Is there a little habit of mine that you’ve been putting up with? Thank you. Would you be willing to tell me gently?
What things between us are “just different, not right or wrong,” which we could stop arguing about starting today?
acts: Today, choose not to correct one of your spouse’s little habits—just bear with it
Name one way your spouse bears with you, and thank them
When you feel impatient, take three deep breaths before you speak
lessons.noon: “with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love” — Lord, right now please lengthen my fuse and widen my heart.

lessons.title: God’s Patience with Me
lessons.theme: Only those who know God’s long patience can learn to be patient with others

v: and refused to obey. They weren’t mindful of your wonders that you did among them, but hardened their neck, and in their rebellion appointed a captain to return to their bondage. But you are a God ready to pardon, gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and didn’t forsake them.
The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some count slowness; but he is patient with us, not wishing that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance.

lessons.still: Think back over your life since you came to faith—how many times has God waited for you to turn back, waited for you to grow? Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, thank you for not giving up on me.” Let this gratitude slowly fill your heart.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled life is lenient with itself and strict with others: my mistakes have reasons; theirs reveal their character. The self-emptied life turns this around and first sees how great a debt it owes God. When I shift from a human point of view to God’s point of view, I discover that being borne with by God is already grace.
lessons.jesus: Looking over Jerusalem, Jesus said, “How often I wanted to gather your children together, like a hen gathers her own brood under her wings” (Luke 13:34). “How often” speaks of his repeated waiting; even when the people were unwilling, his heart stayed open. This is the heart of God’s long patience.
lessons.pray: Gracious and merciful God, thank you for being slow to anger and waiting for us to turn back time after time. We confess that we are lenient with ourselves and strict with our spouse. Help us always remember your patience with us, so that we see our spouse through the same eyes and give each other room to grow in love. Amen.
teach: In Nehemiah’s day, the people looked back on their history, admitted that their ancestors had rebelled again and again, and then said: “But you are a God ready to pardon, gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and didn’t forsake them” (Nehemiah 9:17). “Slow to anger” in Hebrew is literally “long of nose.” The Hebrews pictured anger as steam coming out of the nostrils; a long nose means anger takes a long time to come out.

Peter says, “The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some count slowness; but he is patient with us” (2 Peter 3:9). We often feel God is moving too slowly, but in fact he is giving people time, because he wants “that all should come to repentance.” God’s patience is not permissiveness; it is love giving people room to turn around.

Patience in marriage is first of all not a technique but a memory: remembering how patient God has been with me. When I say to my spouse, “I’ve told you a hundred times,” perhaps I could ask: how many hundreds of times has God told me the same thing? Someone who often remembers God’s patience with them will slowly grow a heart that is patient with others.
q: On my faith journey, which of my weaknesses has God been patient with the longest?
When I compare what I’m impatient with in my spouse to God’s patience with me, how does it feel?
talk: What do you think is the clearest time God has “waited” for you?
In what area would you like me to give you more time instead of pushing you?
acts: Write down one thing God has been patient with you about for a long time, and thank him
Today, say “How many times have I told you?” one less time
Pray for one thing your spouse is working hard to change
lessons.noon: “gracious and merciful, slow to anger” — Lord, right now I remember how patient you are with me—help me be patient with others.

lessons.title: Leave It This Year Also
lessons.theme: Patience is hopeful waiting as our spouse grows

v: He spoke this parable. “A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none.
He said to the vine dresser, ‘Behold, these three years I have come looking for fruit on this fig tree, and found none. Cut it down! Why does it waste the soil?’
He answered, ‘Lord, leave it alone this year also, until I dig around it and fertilize it.
If it bears fruit, fine; but if not, after that, you can cut it down.’”
Better is the end of a thing than its beginning. The patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.

lessons.still: Picture a freshly sown field. Nothing seems to be happening on the surface, but under the soil the seeds are sprouting. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, where I can’t see, you are at work.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Wanting my spouse to change on my timetable is trying to do God’s work in them for him. Let God be God: he decides the pace of growth. My place is the gardener, not the Creator. Changing a mindset takes eight steps, with repeating and correcting along the way, and all of that takes time. We ourselves came the same way.
lessons.jesus: When Jesus healed the blind man at Bethsaida, after the first touch the man said, “I see men, but I see them like walking trees” (Mark 8:24). Jesus wasn’t disappointed; he laid his hands on him again, until he saw everything clearly. Jesus shows us that some change comes in stages, and he is willing to walk with us step by step.
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, thank you for never giving up on us and for giving us time to grow again and again. Give us the patience of the vine dresser—not pushing, not giving up, but tending, watering, and waiting together. Help us notice each other’s small steps forward, and place our timetable for growth in your hands. Amen.
teach: Jesus told a parable: a fig tree had borne no fruit for three years, and the owner said to cut it down. But the vine dresser said, “Lord, leave it alone this year also, until I dig around it and fertilize it” (Luke 13:8). The parable was first a call to repentance, but it also shows us God’s patient heart: one more year, and hands-on care to loosen the soil and feed it. Growth in marriage has its seasons too. Change in our spouse takes time—and so does change in us.

Much disappointment in marriage comes from one expectation: “I’ve told you, so you should change right away.” Yet when we try to change a habit ourselves, it often takes years. The vine dresser’s patience isn’t passive sitting; it’s active companionship: keep praying, keep affirming, keep saying “I noticed” when the other makes small progress. That is how we “dig around it and fertilize it” for our spouse.

The Teacher says, “Better is the end of a thing than its beginning. The patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit” (Ecclesiastes 7:8). The proud look only at the present and want results now; the patient look to the end, trusting that God’s work in their spouse isn’t finished yet. Patience means handing our spouse’s growth timetable back to God.
q: Which change in my spouse am I most impatient about—most tempted to “dig up the seed to check on it”?
Has my spouse made some small progress lately that I haven’t yet noticed or mentioned?
talk: In what area are you working to grow right now? How would you like me to walk with you rather than push you?
Looking back over these years, what do you think has been each of our biggest areas of growth?
acts: Today, name one small recent step forward your spouse has made
Pray once for an area in which your spouse is growing
Tend the plant you planted on the weekend, and remind yourself: growth takes time
lessons.noon: “The patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit” — Lord, right now I place my spouse’s growth in your hands.

lessons.title: Patience Is Not Putting Up with Harm
lessons.theme: Wise patience also knows when to protect ourselves

v: A prudent man sees danger and hides himself; but the simple pass on, and suffer for it.
Saul sought to pin David to the wall with the spear, but he slipped away out of Saul’s presence; and he stuck the spear into the wall. David fled and escaped that night.
Saul sent messengers to David’s house to watch him and to kill him in the morning. Michal, David’s wife, told him, saying, “If you don’t save your life tonight, tomorrow you will be killed.”
So Michal let David down through the window. He went away, fled, and escaped.

lessons.still: Be still and ask yourself honestly: “Am I safe in my home?” Whatever the answer, you can say it out loud before the Lord. He cares for you; he does not want you to carry this alone.
lessons.light: 321 Light: True self-emptying does not mean letting others trample you; it means letting Jesus reign. Letting Jesus reign also means not letting sin reign in the home. The one who abuses needs not more patience but repentance and help; the one who is hurt needs not more patience but safety and protection.
lessons.jesus: When the people of Nazareth tried to throw Jesus off a cliff, “he, passing through the middle of them, went his way” (Luke 4:30). Jesus did not stay to let people harm him, and more than once he slipped away from danger because his time had not yet come. His example tells us that getting away from danger does not conflict with obeying God.
lessons.pray: God our protector, thank you for valuing every person’s life and dignity. Give us patience with good sense—willing to forgive weakness, and wise enough to get away from harm. Protect everyone who is hurt or afraid in their own home. Open a way for them, and give them a safe place and help they can trust. Amen.
teach: Proverbs says, “A prudent man sees danger and hides himself; but the simple pass on, and suffer for it” (Proverbs 22:3). The beauty of patience is a willingness to bear with a spouse’s weaknesses, oversights, and immaturity without keeping score. But biblical patience never asks anyone to stay in danger. The wise see danger and take cover first; this is not a lack of love but God-given good sense.

So we must say this very clearly: physical, verbal, sexual, and financial abuse and control are never things to be patiently endured. Hitting, threats, ongoing humiliation, restricting someone’s movements or money, sexual coercion—these are not “a spouse’s weaknesses”; they are harm. In these situations, continuing to put up with it is not spiritual; it is dangerous. Forgiveness does not mean staying in danger. Safety always comes first.

If you or someone you know is in a situation like this, please contact a trusted pastor, a counselor, or local professional help and protection services as soon as possible. Seeking help is not betraying your marriage, nor is it a lack of faith. When David faced Saul’s spear, “David fled and escaped that night” (1 Samuel 19:10), and Michal even helped him down through a window. Protecting life is exactly what God wants.
q: Have I ever misunderstood “patience” as “swallowing everything”? Where did that idea come from?
Is there a friend or family member near me who may be in an unsafe relationship and needs my care?
talk: For us, what things can we bear with in love? And what are the lines we both agree must never be crossed?
When one of us feels hurt or afraid, how can we say so safely? (If your spouse can’t do this with you right now, or if you feel unsafe, please take this question to a trusted pastor or counselor.)
acts: Note down the contact details of your church’s pastor and a local helpline
Pray for a friend who may be struggling, and reach out with care if needed
Together with your spouse, name one line “our home will never cross”
lessons.noon: “A prudent man sees danger and hides himself” — Lord, right now give me wisdom to protect myself and those I love.

lessons.title: Looking to Jesus, Running with Perseverance
lessons.theme: In the long race of marriage, fix our eyes on Jesus

v: Therefore let’s also, seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let’s run with perseverance the race that is set before us,
looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.
For consider him who has endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, that you don’t grow weary, fainting in your souls.

lessons.still: Imagine you and your spouse running a marathon together, your legs already aching. Look up and see the Lord standing at the finish line, waiting for you. Quietly tell him: “Lord Jesus, we’re looking at you, and we’ll keep running.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keep the focus on Jesus—not on yourself, not on others, not on circumstances. Staring at your spouse’s faults, you grow more tired with every mile; staring at your own grievances, you slow down; looking to Jesus, you find strength to keep going. When we turn from a temporary view to an eternal view, patience finds hope.
lessons.jesus: On the cross, Jesus endured the hostility and mockery of sinners. He could have come down, yet he chose to stay there until he said, “It is finished!” (John 19:30). His endurance was not being trapped; it was choosing to stay because he loved us. When we grow weary in marriage, he is the Lord who has already finished the race and is waiting for us at the finish line.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the author and perfecter of our faith. Thank you for enduring the cross because you love us. Help us lay aside old scores, bitterness, and unrealistic expectations, and run the road of marriage with perseverance. When we are weary and discouraged, let us look up to you and run to the finish together. Amen.
teach: Hebrews says, “let’s run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” (Hebrews 12:1–2). Marriage is not a sprint but a marathon. A sprint takes explosive power; a marathon takes endurance. Many marriages don’t collapse in one great storm; they slowly run out of strength through years of accumulated weariness.

The writer reminds us that before we run, we must “lay aside every weight” (Hebrews 12:1). Marathon runners don’t run carrying luggage. In marriage, old scores, bitterness, comparison, and unrealistic expectations are all heavy luggage. The secret of patience is sometimes not trying harder but putting down what we don’t need to carry, so we can run lighter.

Most important of all is “looking to Jesus.” Jesus, “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame” (Hebrews 12:2). His endurance had a direction, because he saw the joy ahead. This week we have learned that patience begins with humility, that we remember God’s patience, wait like a farmer, wisely protect safety, and look to Jesus to finish the race. Next week we taste the fifth flavor: kindness.
q: In the long race of marriage, what unnecessary “luggage” am I carrying right now?
When I’ve been weary lately, have my eyes been mostly on my spouse, on myself, or on Jesus?
talk: If our marriage right now were a marathon, which stretch would we be on: the start, the middle miles, an uphill climb, or a tailwind?
Which lesson on patience this week helped you most? What one piece of “luggage” do we want to put down together?
acts: Write down one piece of “luggage” you want to put down, and hand it to the Lord
Today, tell your spouse: “Thank you for running this race with me.”
Before bed, read Hebrews 12:2 together
lessons.noon: “looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” — Lord Jesus, right now I turn my eyes from the difficulty to you.

mem.t: And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

s: Together, find a piggy bank or small box and name it “Our Love Deposits.”
Each of you write down three small things that would make you feel treated with kindness (“If you did this, I’d feel cared for”), then swap notes.
Agree that each day this week you’ll each do at least one thing from the other’s note, and drop a coin in the jar when you’ve done it.
At the end of the week, count your deposits together and pray, thanking God for the fruit of kindness he is growing in your home.

lessons.title: First Put Away, Then Be Kind
lessons.theme: Kindness grows in a heart cleared of bitterness

v: Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice.
And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

lessons.still: Picture a flower bed overgrown with weeds. To plant new flowers, you first have to pull out the weeds. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, what weeds in my heart are keeping kindness from growing?”
