lessons.light: 321 Light: Bitterness is the fruit of the self-ruled life: my grievances, my rights that were violated. The tighter I hold on, the more bitter my heart becomes. Being self-emptied doesn’t mean pretending I wasn’t hurt; it means handing the hurt to God and not letting bitterness rule in my heart. When we let Jesus reign, kindness has room to grow.
lessons.jesus: Some people carried a paralyzed man on a mat to Jesus. The first thing Jesus said was, “Son, cheer up! Your sins are forgiven you” (Matthew 9:2). He didn’t begin by listing the man’s past; he used a warm word that put him at ease. Jesus’ kindness makes people feel lighter—and makes them want to be better.
lessons.pray: Lord, search our hearts and put away from us all bitterness, wrath, and anger. We don’t want weeds to choke our home. Plant kindness in our hearts, so that in how we treat each other, our spouse feels lighter and accepted, just as we are before you. Amen.
teach: Before Paul says “be kind,” he says, “Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice” (Ephesians 4:31). There’s an order here: first put away, then be kind. Just as in a flower bed, if you don’t pull the weeds first, the flowers you plant will soon be choked out. Someone who harbors bitterness finds it very hard to be truly kind to their spouse.

These six words trace a downward path: bitterness is a sourness inside; wrath is resentment that keeps simmering; anger is the explosion; outcry is the shouting match; slander is running the other person down behind their back; malice is the intent to hurt. Many family conflicts start with just a little bitterness and slide all the way down. The sooner we deal with it at the source, the easier it is to turn back.

Then Paul says, “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32). The Greek word for “kind” carries the sense of mild, easy, pleasant to be around. When Jesus said, “my yoke is easy” (Matthew 11:30), the word “easy” comes from the same root. Kind people make those around them feel lighter, not weighed down.
q: Of the six words Paul lists, which shows up most often in my heart? What usually sets it off?
Am I someone who makes my spouse feel “at ease” or “weighed down”?
talk: When do you feel most at ease with me? When do you feel pressure? Please say it gently.
Is there a “weed of bitterness” in our home that we could pray about and pull out together?
acts: Write down something that has left a sour taste in your heart, and place it before the Lord
Today, avoid criticizing your spouse in front of others
Do one small thing that makes your spouse feel at ease
lessons.noon: “be kind to one another, tender hearted” — Lord, right now pull the bitterness out of my heart and let me treat others with kindness.

lessons.title: God Was Kind to Me First
lessons.theme: The source of kindness is the kindness God shows to the undeserving

v: But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us,
even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved—
and raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus,
that in the ages to come he might show the exceeding riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus;

lessons.still: Think back to what you were like before you knew the Lord, or to your least lovable moment. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, even then, you were already kind to me.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Those who have received God’s kindness find it easiest to be kind to others; those who forget the grace they received find it easiest to demand from others. The self-ruled life often assumes, “I deserved it anyway”; the self-emptied life knows, “It’s all grace.” When a life changes, relationships change.
lessons.jesus: At the gate of the town of Nain, Jesus saw a widow on her way to bury her only son. Scripture says, “When the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, ‘Don’t cry’” (Luke 7:13). The widow hadn’t asked him for anything, yet Jesus stopped on his own initiative. Jesus’ kindness sees people’s needs first and reaches out first.
lessons.pray: God our Savior, thank you for showing us your kindness when we least deserved it. We confess that we often forget how we received grace, and so we demand much of our spouse and give little kindness. Help us remember your mercy, and treat each other with the same kindness. Amen.
teach: Paul is very frank about what we used to be: “dead through our trespasses” (Ephesians 2:5). The dead can do nothing for themselves; they can’t please God or improve themselves. This isn’t describing other people; it’s describing you and me. When God met us, we were not lovable, and we had nothing to offer in exchange.

Then the passage turns: “But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us” (Ephesians 2:4), made us alive together with Christ. “But God” are two of the most beautiful words in the whole Bible. Paul says God did this so “that in the ages to come he might show the exceeding riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:7). Our lives, saved by grace, are themselves a display case of God’s kindness.

This changes how we see our spouse. We often say, “I’ll be good to them when they’re good to me.” That is transactional kindness. God’s kindness, though, is given first and is undeserved. When I remember how I received grace, I’m more able to be kind to my spouse even when they’re not at their best or doing well. The power to be kind comes from the memory of having been treated kindly.
q: At my least lovable, how was God kind to me? Do I still remember how that moved me?
Has my kindness toward my spouse quietly turned into a “transaction”?
talk: Was there a time when you were still kind to me even when I was at my worst? What did that mean to me?
When one of us is exhausted or in a bad mood, how do you most need me to be kind to you?
acts: Write down a time in the past when you deeply experienced God’s kindness
Today, when your spouse is struggling, ask first: “How can I help you?”
Let go of one “I’ll be good to them when they’re good to me” thought
lessons.noon: “But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us” — Lord, right now I remember your mercy, and I want to show mercy to others.

lessons.title: Leaving a Little Extra Grain
lessons.theme: Kindness often hides in small, unnoticed things

v: At meal time Boaz said to her, “Come here, and eat some bread, and dip your morsel in the vinegar.” She sat beside the reapers, and they passed her parched grain. She ate, was satisfied, and left some of it.
When she had risen up to glean, Boaz commanded his young men, saying, “Let her glean even among the sheaves, and don’t reproach her.
Also pull out some for her from the bundles, and leave it. Let her glean, and don’t rebuke her.”

lessons.still: Think of the last time someone did something small for you that warmed your heart. Quietly thank the Lord, and ask him: “What kind of extra handful of grain could I leave for my spouse today?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The self-ruled life keeps score in small things—“That’s not my job.” The self-emptied life sees small things as chances to love. Kindness isn’t an occasional grand gesture; it’s making our spouse feel seen and protected in everyday small things.
lessons.jesus: A woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years secretly touched Jesus’ clothing. When she was discovered, she fell trembling at his feet. Jesus said to her, “Daughter, cheer up. Your faith has made you well. Go in peace” (Luke 8:48). In front of everyone, Jesus restored her dignity. His kindness always cares for a person’s honor and heart.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for the unnoticed graces you keep leaving in our lives. Give us thoughtful hearts to be kind to our spouse in everyday small things—protecting their dignity, providing for their needs, and helping them feel treasured at home. May our home be a Boaz’s field for each other. Amen.
teach: Ruth was a widow and a foreigner, gleaning ears of grain in Boaz’s field to feed her mother-in-law. Boaz not only let her glean, but told his workers: “Also pull out some for her from the bundles, and leave it. Let her glean, and don’t rebuke her” (Ruth 2:16). This was quiet, thoughtful kindness: leaving a little extra grain without making her feel like a charity case.

Boaz did other small things too. At mealtime he invited her over: “Come here, and eat some bread, and dip your morsel in the vinegar” (Ruth 2:14). He also instructed his workers, “don’t reproach her” (Ruth 2:15). Kindness is often not a grand gesture but a thoughtful heart: protecting the other person’s dignity, providing what they need, making sure they are seen.

Kindness in marriage is often “leaving a little extra grain” too: remembering your spouse’s favorite flavor and picking up an extra one; seeing they’re tired and taking over the dishes; saving their face in front of family and friends; gently reminding them when they forget, instead of teasing. These small things may seem insignificant, but they are how our spouse comes to feel treasured at home.
q: Have I recently told my spouse, about some small matter, “That’s not my problem”?
In what small things does my spouse most need their dignity protected, or to be seen?
talk: What small thing I did recently made you feel especially warm?
In front of family, friends, or the kids, how would you like me to “save your face”?
acts: Today, pick up one little extra thing your spouse likes
Take over a small household chore your spouse usually does
Say something affirming about your spouse in front of others
lessons.noon: “Let her glean, and don’t rebuke her” — Lord, right now let me be kind to my spouse with gentle words and small actions.

lessons.title: Love Deposits
lessons.theme: Every small kindness is love deposited in our marriage

v: Don’t let kindness and truth forsake you. Bind them around your neck. Write them on the tablet of your heart.
So you will find favor, and good understanding in the sight of God and man.
The liberal soul shall be made fat. He who waters shall be watered also himself.

lessons.still: Imagine your marriage has an invisible account, and every gentle word makes a deposit. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, lately have I been making deposits or withdrawals?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled life sees only how much it has deposited and calculates, “I’ve given so much—how much has my spouse paid back?” The self-emptied life makes deposits out of love, not to earn interest. We deposit because God first filled our account with grace; we are simply transferring his kindness onward.
lessons.jesus: On the eve of his suffering, Jesus told his disciples, “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22:15). In his final hours, he chose to share a table with them. Three years of walking and eating together were the love he deposited into his disciples’ lives, and it carried them through their darkest hours later on.
lessons.pray: Lord full of kindness, thank you for filling our lives with grace. Help us write kindness and truth on the tablets of our hearts and make deposits of kindness for each other every day. When we give and see no response, keep us from losing heart. We trust that whoever waters others will be watered, and that you will bring a harvest in our home. Amen.
teach: We can think of marriage as a “love account.” Every kind word, thoughtful act, and tender hug is a deposit; every sarcastic remark, forgotten promise, and harsh tone is a withdrawal. When the account is well stocked, the relationship can handle an occasional withdrawal. But if we only withdraw and never deposit, even one small comment can leave the account “overdrawn.”

Proverbs says, “Don’t let kindness and truth forsake you. Bind them around your neck. Write them on the tablet of your heart” (Proverbs 3:3). The Hebrew word for “kindness” here is hesed, God’s covenant love—kindness that holds on to the end. Binding it around the neck keeps it always in sight; writing it on the heart makes it part of who we are. Kindness is not an occasional mood but a habit engraved into our lives.

Proverbs also says, “The liberal soul shall be made fat. He who waters shall be watered also himself” (Proverbs 11:25). Sometimes we make many deposits but see no response, and we lose heart. But the heart that waters others will not dry up, and deposits of kindness are never wasted; God will bring the harvest in his time. Those closest to us need our kindness most, yet are often the ones we overlook.
q: This past week, have I made more deposits or more withdrawals in our “love account”?
Have I made many deposits without seeing a response, and started to lose heart or keep score?
talk: For you, what feels most like a “deposit”? What feels most like a “withdrawal”?
For this week’s kindness jar, what kind of deposit would you most like to receive from me?
acts: Today, do three small “deposit” things for your spouse
Avoid one “withdrawal” comment that could hurt your spouse
Drop a coin in the kindness jar and say why
lessons.noon: “He who waters shall be watered also himself” — Lord, right now I won’t lose heart. I’ll keep making deposits of kindness for my spouse.

lessons.title: Merciful Like the Father
lessons.theme: Kindness at its fullest is kindness to the ungrateful

v: But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing back; and your reward will be great, and you will be children of the Most High; for he is kind toward the unthankful and evil.
“Therefore be merciful, even as your Father is also merciful.
The merciful man does good to his own soul, but he who is cruel troubles his own flesh.

lessons.still: Think of the Father’s face as he looks at you, his eyes full of mercy. Quietly tell him: “Father, let my eyes be like yours, looking at my spouse with mercy.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: From a human point of view, my spouse doesn’t deserve it; from God’s point of view, I don’t deserve it either—yet I have received kindness. When my focus moves from my spouse’s performance to the Father’s mercy, I can treat others as he does. One purpose: to build a household that belongs to God—and the clearest mark of such a household is kindness.
lessons.jesus: Someone cut off the ear of the high priest’s servant—one of the men who had come to arrest Jesus. Yet Jesus “touched his ear and healed him” (Luke 22:51). In the very moment he was betrayed and seized, Jesus was still kind to those who opposed him. He shows us what the Father’s mercy looks like.
lessons.pray: Merciful Father, thank you for being kind to the ungrateful, and kind to us. Make our hearts like yours, so that we are still kind to our spouse even when there is no response. Thank you for the fruit you have grown in our home these five weeks. Keep working, and fill our home with love, joy, peace, patience, and kindness, to show your glory. Amen.
teach: Jesus said the Father “is kind toward the unthankful and evil” (Luke 6:35), so “be merciful, even as your Father is also merciful” (Luke 6:36). This is kindness at its highest standard: being kind not only to those who are good to me, but also to those who give nothing back. Sometimes in marriage we give, and our spouse doesn’t say thank you—or even complains. That is exactly when we learn to be like the Father.

Proverbs says, “The merciful man does good to his own soul, but he who is cruel troubles his own flesh” (Proverbs 11:17). Kindness isn’t only for the other person; it’s for us too. Someone who nurses bitterness and keeps score everywhere wounds their own heart first; someone who chooses kindness finds their heart set free. Kindness and forgiveness walk the same road. But we must be clear: forgiveness and kindness never mean tolerating harm. If there is violence or control in the home, safety comes first—seek help from a pastor and from professionals.

Over these five weeks we have tasted the first five flavors of the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, and kindness. They are one fruit, growing through the practice of 920: my spouse is my most important “2”; in Christ I practice the “0” of self-emptying; and the Spirit bears the “9”-fold fruit in our home. Four more flavors are waiting for us, so let’s keep growing together.
q: Was there a recent time I was kind to my spouse and wasn’t thanked? What went through my mind?
Looking back over these five weeks, which flavor of the ninefold fruit has grown most visibly in me? Which most needs the Spirit to keep working?
talk: Over these five weeks, which fruit have you seen growing in me? Please name one specific thing.

In the next four weeks (goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control), which fruit are you most hoping to see grow in our home? (If your spouse can’t join you right now, write down your prayer for them.)
acts: Today, be kind to your spouse without expecting anything back
Count the kindness jar together and give thanks for this week
Write down the one change from these five weeks you are most grateful for
lessons.noon: “be merciful, even as your Father is also merciful” — Father, right now let me see my spouse through your mercy.

mem.t: In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another,

s: At the start of the weekend, each of you quietly decide on one good thing you will do for the other in secret—don’t say what it is yet.
Over the weekend, quietly do it: perhaps polish their shoes, mend a piece of clothing, or tidy their desk.
Before the weekend ends, have a cup of tea together. Take turns guessing what the other did for you, then share how it felt to be treated with such goodness.
Read Romans 12:10 together, and say to each other: “Thank you for honoring me and putting me first.” Then pray together for your home.

lessons.title: Goodness Comes from God
lessons.theme: Once we have tasted God’s goodness, we can bring goodness home

v: Oh taste and see that the LORD is good. Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him.
As he was going out into the way, one ran to him, knelt before him, and asked him, “Good Teacher, what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?”
Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one—God.

lessons.still: Be still and recall the last time you thought, “God is so good”—maybe just a hot meal or a good night’s sleep. Tell the Lord: “Lord, you are good. Today I want to taste your goodness first, then bring it to my family.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Goodness from the self-ruled life is a transaction: “I’m good to you so you’ll be good to me.” As soon as there’s no response, goodwill turns into resentment. Goodness from the self-emptied life is received from God and then freely given; the focus is on Jesus, not on whether my spouse pays me back.
lessons.jesus: The book of Acts describes Jesus as one “who went about doing good” (Acts 10:38). His goodness was not a slogan but something he did all along the way: touching lepers, feeding the hungry, giving a weeping widow back her son. Jesus shows us that goodness is God’s character put into action.
lessons.pray: Good Father, thank you for treating us well every day with so much grace, seen and unseen. We confess that our goodness is often limited and mixed with calculation. Let us taste your goodness daily and be filled with it, so that at home we freely give away your goodness. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
teach: You only know whether an apple is sweet by biting into it; looking at a picture isn’t enough. The psalmist says, “Oh taste and see that the LORD is good” (Psalm 34:8). He isn’t inviting us to study God’s goodness but to taste it for ourselves. The fruit of goodness doesn’t start with trying hard to be a good person; it starts with experiencing how good God is.

A man ran up and called Jesus “Good Teacher,” but Jesus answered, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one—God” (Mark 10:18). Jesus wasn’t denying his own goodness; he was turning the man’s eyes back to the source: true goodness is found only in God. Our own goodness is often mixed with the calculation, “I’ve done so much—you ought to be good to me too.” God’s goodness is pure and asks nothing in return.

This is great news for marriage. After years together, it can feel as if our “supply of goodness” has run dry and we can’t squeeze out one more pleasant look. But goodness is fruit the Spirit bears, not something we squeeze out of ourselves. When we return to God each day to taste his goodness, those who have been treated well by him will naturally treat well those around them. A changed life changes how we live.
q: When was the last time I personally “tasted” God’s goodness?
How much of my kindness toward my spouse carries the calculation “you ought to be good to me too”?
talk: Share a small thing this week that made you think, “God is so good.”
What have I done that made you feel I was truly good to you? How did you feel at that moment?
acts: Write down three small things today that made you think, “God is so good”
Tell your spouse: “Thank you. Today you were so good to me when you...”
Do one small thing for your spouse without expecting anything in return
lessons.noon: “Oh taste and see that the LORD is good” — Lord, right now let me taste your goodness, so that I can treat those around me well.

lessons.title: Tender Affection, Outdoing One Another in Honor
lessons.theme: Goodness is love without pretense that races to put the other first

v: Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor that which is evil. Cling to that which is good.
In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another,
not lagging in diligence, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord,
rejoicing in hope, enduring in troubles, continuing steadfastly in prayer,
contributing to the needs of the saints, and given to hospitality.

lessons.still: Place your hand on your chest and be still for a moment. Ask the Lord: “Lord, is there anywhere my love for my spouse is only on the surface, only an act?” You don’t need to answer right away; let the Holy Spirit gently shine his light on you.
lessons.light: 321 Light: At home, the proud compete for position: who’s right, who should give in first, who works harder. The humble compete for opportunities: who can honor first, who can serve first. Pride provokes pride, and both lose; yielding inspires yielding, and both win.
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I am among you as one who serves” (Luke 22:27). While the disciples were arguing about who was the greatest, Jesus picked up a towel and washed their feet himself. He didn’t wait for them to honor him first; he bent down first. This is the most beautiful picture of “in honor prefer one another.”
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the King of kings, yet you are among us as one who serves. Remove the pretense from our love, and make us tenderly affectionate at home, outdoing one another in honor. Help us stop arguing about who’s right and who’s wrong, and instead race to honor and to serve, so that our home is filled with real warmth. Amen.
teach: When Paul describes a life of goodness, his first line is: “Let love be without hypocrisy” (Romans 12:9). The Greek word for hypocrisy originally described an actor on stage wearing a mask. Marriage has masks too: loving in front of others, cold at home; saying “fine” while keeping score inside. The first step of goodness is to take off the mask and let love be real.

Paul goes on: “In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another” (Romans 12:10). “Tenderly affectionate” describes the natural warmth and affection of family. “In honor prefer one another” carries the sense of leading the way in showing honor—racing to respect the other first. Picture a door with two people each hurrying to hold it open so the other can go first. That’s a picture of a good home: not arguing over who deserves respect first, but competing to see who can show respect first.

The goodness in this passage is very concrete: “not lagging in diligence” and “given to hospitality” (Romans 12:11, 13). At home, that means not pushing all the chores onto the other person, stepping in when they’re tired, and welcoming our spouse as the most honored guest in our house. Goodness is not a feeling; it’s a string of good deeds we race each other to do.
q: In our marriage, do I more often compete for position or for opportunities?
Is there a setting where my attitude toward my spouse in public is very different from at home?
talk: If I treated you as the most honored guest in our home, how would you most like me to welcome you?
Lately, in what way do you feel I’ve put you first and made you feel respected?
acts: Today, beat your spouse to a household chore they usually handle
At mealtime, serve your spouse the best portion first
Thank your spouse in the tone you would use with an honored guest
lessons.noon: “in honor prefer one another” — Lord, right now let me race to honor others rather than compete for position.

lessons.title: Created for Good Works
lessons.theme: God has prepared good works for us to walk in at home

v: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.
Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.
So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good toward all men, and especially toward those who are of the household of the faith.

lessons.still: Quietly think through the places you will pass through at home today: the kitchen, the dinner table, the bedside. Tell the Lord: “Lord, you have already prepared good works for me in these places. Open my eyes to see them.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change your mindset and your life will change. If we see chores as “my burden,” we feel more and more hard done by; if we see them as “good works God prepared for me,” they become more and more meaningful. When we shift from a human point of view to God’s, the same small task takes on eternal value.
lessons.jesus: Passing under Zacchaeus’s tree, Jesus stopped and said, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house” (Luke 19:5). In a man everyone despised, he saw a good work God had prepared. Jesus shows us that good people have eyes that see opportunities—they stop where others walk on by.
lessons.pray: God our Creator, thank you for re-creating us in Christ as your workmanship, and for preparing good works for us to do. Open our eyes to the small opportunities in our home. When we grow weary in doing good, strengthen us so we don’t lose heart or give up, for in due season we will reap. Amen.
teach: Paul says, “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Ephesians 2:10). The word “workmanship” carries the sense of a work of art, a masterpiece. God has re-created us as his masterpiece, and one purpose is good works. Just as a fine violin is made to play beautiful music, a person renewed by Christ is made to live a beautiful life.

Even more wonderful, these are good works “which God prepared before that we would walk in them” (Ephesians 2:10). God hasn’t handed us a heavy to-do list. Like a loving father, he has set gifts along the path ahead of time, waiting for us to pick them up. Maybe it’s a cup of hot tea when your spouse gets home from work, maybe a word of encouragement when they’re feeling low. Goodness is often not about finding big things to do, but seeing the small things God has already placed in front of us.

But doing good can wear us out, especially at home, where our efforts often go unseen. So Paul encourages us: “Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up” (Galatians 6:9). He adds, “especially toward those who are of the household of the faith” (Galatians 6:10)—and that surely begins with the household we share. We often save our best goodwill for outsiders and leave our most worn-out selves for family. The practice of goodness has to start with the one closest to us.
q: What good work might God have prepared in our home that I’ve been missing?
Do I give my best goodwill to outsiders and leave my most worn-out self for my spouse?
talk: When are you most tired at home lately, and most in need of a helping hand?
Let’s think together: what good deed could we do together this month for family or neighbors?
acts: Today, watch for one small good work God has prepared, and do it
At the time your spouse is most tired, step in and take over a task
Save your gentlest tone for the first words you say when you get home today
lessons.noon: “Let’s not be weary in doing good” — Lord, right now, tired as I am, I still want to do good to my family.

lessons.title: Doing Good Where No One Sees
lessons.theme: The Father sees the good we do in secret

v: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.

Therefore, when you do merciful deeds, don’t sound a trumpet before yourself, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may get glory from men. Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward.
But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does,
so that your merciful deeds may be in secret, then your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.

lessons.still: Imagine the Father gently watching you as you do housework alone, when no one notices. Quietly tell him: “Father, thank you for seeing what I give in secret. Today I want to do it for you alone.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled life needs an audience to do good; if no one sees, it doesn’t seem worth it. The self-emptied life needs only one audience: God. To let Jesus receive all the glory means finishing the task without signing our name to it.
lessons.jesus: After healing a man with leprosy, Jesus told him, “See that you say nothing to anybody” (Mark 1:44). He did many miracles yet often stepped aside, not seeking people’s praise. His greatest act of goodness was completed on the cross, where onlookers saw only shame, not glory. Jesus’ goodness never needed applause.
lessons.pray: Father who sees in secret, thank you for seeing every unnoticed thing we give. Purify our motives for doing good, so that we no longer need applause or keep a tab. Let us love and serve quietly where the other cannot see, so that our home is like a deep-rooted tree, steady and blessed. Amen.
teach: The most important part of a great tree is its roots, buried underground where no one sees them. Marriage is the same. What really makes a home steady is often not the big anniversary surprise, but countless unseen acts of goodness: pulling the covers over your spouse in the middle of the night, quietly saving the food they love, speaking well of them in front of others.

Jesus said, “don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matthew 6:3). It’s a vivid way of saying: when you do good, you don’t even need to keep remembering it yourself. In marriage, what hurts most is not failing to do things, but doing them and then constantly reminding: “Look how much I’ve done for you!” Then the good deed becomes an IOU.

Jesus also said, “your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly” (Matthew 6:4). We can rest assured that no small thing done out of love is wasted; the Father sees it all. When we no longer need our spouse’s applause, we are truly free to love. And wonderfully, hidden goodness is often the most moving, because it carries the fragrance of the Father.
q: Among the things I do for my spouse, which ones have I been quietly “keeping a tab” on?
If no one saw, which good things would I still be willing to keep doing?
talk: Have you ever discovered something I did for you in secret? How did it make you feel?
Is there something you’ve been doing quietly that you think I may not have noticed? Let me thank you today.
acts: Today, do something for your spouse in secret, and don’t mention it
Thank your spouse for something they’ve been quietly doing all along
Tear up one inner IOU of “what I’ve done for you,” and hand it to God
lessons.noon: “your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly” — Father, right now I do good for you alone; I don’t need applause.

lessons.title: Overcome Evil with Good
lessons.theme: When we are wronged, goodness is the overcoming response

v: Repay no one evil for evil. Respect what is honorable in the sight of all men.
If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.
Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.”
Therefore “If your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him a drink; for in doing so, you will heap coals of fire on his head.”
Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

lessons.still: Recall the last time you felt wronged or misunderstood at home. Don’t rush to defend yourself. Gently place that hurt in the Lord’s hands and say: “Lord, teach me the way to overcome.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Repaying evil for evil is the self on the throne: “You hurt me, so I’ll get even.” Overcoming evil with good is letting Jesus reign: “Vengeance belongs to the Lord; my part is to do good.” Laying down the right to get even and returning to our rightful place is humility, and humility inspires humility. That is often where revival in a family begins.
lessons.jesus: Nailed to the cross, enduring the greatest injustice, Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). He did not repay evil for evil but overcame sin with love and forgiveness. The cross is the greatest victory of good over evil.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, on the cross you overcame evil with good, and you overcame our sin too. Forgive us for the times we have repaid evil for evil and refused to give way. When we are wronged, help us leave justice in your hands and respond with goodness. And protect everyone in our home, so that our home becomes a safe, warm place where we treat each other well. Amen.
teach: The most common cycle between spouses goes like this: you go cold, so I go cold; you get loud, so I get louder. Paul says, “Repay no one evil for evil” (Romans 12:17). Repaying evil for evil is like two people throwing mud at each other: in the end both are filthy and the house is a mess. Goodness is the first one to put the mud down.

Paul concludes: “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21). Repaying evil for evil looks like fighting back, but in fact it means evil has beaten me, because I’ve let the other person’s wrong decide my response. Overcoming evil with good means letting the Holy Spirit, not the other person’s emotions, decide how I respond. When my spouse says something cutting, I can choose not to cut back, and say calmly: “That made me a bit sad. Can we talk this through?”

But let’s be clear: overcoming evil with good does not mean tolerating harm. Paul says, “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men” (Romans 12:18), which means peace is sometimes not within our control. If there is physical, verbal, sexual, or financial abuse and control in the home, that is not something to endure with “goodness.” Safety comes first, and forgiveness does not mean staying in danger. Seek help from a pastor and from professionals right away, and contact local protection services when needed.
q: The last time my spouse’s words stung, what was my first reaction?
In which recurring conflict could I be the first to put down the mud?
talk: What topic most easily pulls us into tit-for-tat? Could we agree on a signal to pause next time?
Looking back on this week, what fruit of goodness have you seen in me? If your spouse can’t join you right now, write down one thing you’d like to thank them for.
acts: Next time you want to snap back, take a deep breath and say something gentle
Agree with your spouse on a pause signal for times of conflict
Pray about a time you were wronged, and entrust it to God
lessons.noon: “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” — Lord, right now help me respond with goodness and not be overcome by evil.

mem.t: They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.

s: Get paper and pens. Each of you write down three moments in your marriage when “God did not abandon us,” then take turns sharing.
Each of you name one thing the other “said and then did” that gave you a deep sense of security, and thank them specifically.
Together, set a small commitment you can keep next week (for example, a walk together on Wednesday). Write it on the calendar and check on it next week.
Read Lamentations 3:22–23 together and declare as one: “They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:23).

lessons.title: New Every Morning
lessons.theme: God’s faithfulness is the foundation of faithfulness in marriage

v: This I recall to my mind; therefore I have hope.
It is because of the LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail.
They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.
“The LORD is my portion,” says my soul. “Therefore I will hope in him.”

lessons.still: You woke this morning, breathed, opened your eyes, and everything around you was a new day again. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, thank you for coming again this morning. Your faithfulness has never once been late.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Human faithfulness rises and falls with our emotions, because the self-ruled life is loyal only to “my feelings.” When our focus shifts from self to God, from the temporary to the eternal, we stop asking only, “Do I still feel it?” and start asking, “How does the faithful God want me to keep my covenant today?”
lessons.jesus: John says of Jesus, “having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John 13:1). That night, Judas would betray him, Peter would deny him, and the other disciples would run away. Jesus knew it all, yet he loved them to the end. Jesus’ faithfulness didn’t depend on his disciples being reliable; it flowed from who he is—faithful.
lessons.pray: Faithful God, thank you that your loving kindness is new every morning. In our days of failure, weariness, and cooling feelings, you have never left. Let our marriage be built not on changing feelings but on your unchanging faithfulness. Let us receive it from you, and live it out toward each other. Amen.
teach: Lamentations is a book written among ruins. Jerusalem had been destroyed, its gates burned, its people taken captive. Yet right in the middle of the darkest chapter, the prophet says, “This I recall to my mind; therefore I have hope” (Lamentations 3:21). What he recalled was not his own strength but God’s character. When a marriage hits hard times, this is what we most need to recall too.

He says that God’s loving kindnesses and mercies “are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:23). “Faithfulness” here means steady and dependable, like a rock that cannot be crushed. The sun never goes on strike and refuses to rise today just because clouds covered it yesterday. God’s love for us doesn’t depend on how well we did yesterday; it arrives fresh every morning.

This is the foundation of faithfulness in marriage. If a couple’s loyalty rests only on their feelings—faithful when the feelings are strong, wavering when they fade—the marriage is built on sand. But when we first receive God’s faithfulness each day, we have strength to be faithful to our spouse. We can keep our covenant not because we are so reliable, but because the God who made a covenant with us never breaks his word.
q: Is my loyalty in marriage built more on my feelings or on God’s faithfulness?
Thinking back on a hard season in our marriage, where did God’s faithfulness hold me up?
talk: In our marriage, what is your most unforgettable experience of “God did not abandon us”?
Was there a day recently when you especially needed the promise that his mercies are “new every morning”?
acts: When you get up in the morning, first tell God: “Thank you for your faithfulness.”
Write down one way God has faithfully held up your marriage
Tell your spouse: “Thank you for staying by my side all these years.”
lessons.noon: “They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness” — Faithful Lord, right now I give today to you; you never break your word.

lessons.title: Let Your Yes Be Yes
lessons.theme: Faithfulness means doing what we say, even when it costs us

v: But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one.
in whose eyes a vile man is despised, but who honors those who fear the LORD; he who keeps an oath even when it hurts, and doesn’t change;

lessons.still: Think back over the things you have already promised people today, big and small. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, make my ‘yes’ a real ‘yes,’ so that my family can rely on my word with confidence.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Behind frequently broken promises there is often the self-ruled life: I keep my word only when it’s convenient, and when it isn’t, my own needs jump to the front of the line. Self-emptied faithfulness puts “I promised you” ahead of “what I want right now.” People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than convenience.
lessons.jesus: Jesus “intently set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51), because he knew it was the mission the Father had entrusted to him, even with the cross ahead. In the end he could say, “I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do” (John 17:4). Jesus did what he said, and no cost could make him change.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you accomplished everything the Father entrusted to you, and every word you speak can be trusted. Forgive us for the many times we have promised lightly and not followed through. Help us speak honestly, promise carefully, and do our best to finish what we’ve agreed to. Let our “yes” be a “yes” the other can lean on with confidence. Amen.
teach: Whether a check is worth anything depends not on the number written on it but on whether there’s money in the bank. The words we say to our spouse are checks too: “I’ll be home by seven,” “I’ll spend this weekend with you,” “I’ll change.” If they keep bouncing, however nice our words sound, our spouse no longer dares to cash them.

Jesus said, “But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37). In those days people used all sorts of oaths to add weight to their words, as if anything said without an oath could be discounted. But Jesus said every word of God’s people should be reliable, needing no extra guarantee. At home, that means doing what we’ve agreed to do, saying honestly when we can’t, and not brushing our spouse off with “Yeah, yeah, sure.”

The psalm describes the person God welcomes as one “who keeps an oath even when it hurts, and doesn’t change” (Psalm 15:4). Our wedding covenant is an oath we made before God and many witnesses. Over time, keeping it can feel costly: we have to set aside our own plans and give more patience. But it is exactly this kind of faithfulness—keeping our word even when it hurts—that gives our spouse’s heart a place to rest.
q: What is the most recent promise to my spouse that “bounced”? Why didn’t I follow through?
Do I often brush my spouse off with “Yeah, yeah, sure”? What attitude lies behind that?
talk: What is something I said and then did that made you feel especially secure?
Is there a small promise I often make but don’t keep? Please tell me gently—I want to start again.
acts: Today, only promise what you’re sure you can do
Finish one small thing you promised your spouse but haven’t yet done
If you can’t do something, say so honestly and up front, without making excuses
lessons.noon: “let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’” — Lord, right now make my words honest and reliable.

lessons.title: Faithful in the Smallest Things
lessons.theme: Great trust is built up from small things

v: He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.
If therefore you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches?
If you have not been faithful in that which is another’s, who will give you that which is your own?
Many men claim to be men of unfailing love, but who can find a faithful man?

lessons.still: Look at something small near you: a cup, a key, a pen. Quietly wonder: does God care about things this small too? Tell the Lord: “Lord, today I want to be faithful to you in small things.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: In the practice of 920 (my spouse is my most important “2”; practice the “0” of self-emptying; bear the “9”-fold fruit), faithfulness is an “unremarkable” fruit, yet it is the foundation of every relationship. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: faithfulness in small things at home is the very training ground for the greater ministry God will entrust to us later.
lessons.jesus: Even in his extreme agony on the cross, Jesus remembered his mother and entrusted her to the disciple he loved: “Woman, behold, your son!” (John 19:26). While accomplishing the great work of redemption, he did not overlook the needs of those beside him. Jesus was faithful in the greatest matter, and faithful in what seemed small.
lessons.pray: Lord, you value the smallest things, and you are faithful to us even in the smallest things. Help us be faithful with our time, our money, our words, and our small promises. Shine your light on every place we have hidden or been careless, and make us willing to be open. Let our trust in each other be built up day by day. Amen.
teach: How does a piggy bank get filled? Not with one big sum dropped in at once, but coin by coin. Trust in marriage works the same way. Replying to messages promptly, remembering what your spouse asked you to do, keeping the finances clear, not being late when you’ve agreed on a time—these seem trivial, but bit by bit they build the trust that says, “I can safely entrust myself to you.”

Jesus said, “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10). We think that only when a big test comes can you tell whether someone is faithful, but Jesus says the real score was set long before, in the small things. Someone who is sloppy in small matters, vague about small sums of money, and careless about small lies will find it very hard to stand firm when a big temptation comes.

Proverbs sighs, “Many men claim to be men of unfailing love, but who can find a faithful man?” (Proverbs 20:6). It’s easy to say how much we love our family; being faithful day after day is rare. The good news is that faithfulness doesn’t need to wait for a big occasion. There are many small opportunities today: a phone with nothing to hide, spending with nothing concealed, promises written down. Every small act of faithfulness is a coin dropped into the piggy bank of trust in our marriage.
q: In what small things have I not been faithful enough or clear enough with my spouse?
Do I have some “little secrets” that, while not big, keep me from being fully open?
talk: In what small thing do you feel I’m very reliable?
Is there a small area in our home (time, money, phones, chores) where we could agree to be a little more open with each other?
acts: Today, do one small thing you told your spouse you’d do, on time
Tell your spouse about a recent purchase, without being asked
When you reply to your spouse’s messages, don’t put it off or give a careless answer
lessons.noon: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” — Lord, right now let me be faithful to you in the small things at hand.

lessons.title: Trust Can Be Rebuilt
lessons.theme: Broken trust is slowly repaired through sincere repentance and time

v: He who conceals his sins doesn’t prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy.

Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance, and don’t begin to say among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham for our father;’ for I tell you that God is able to raise up children to Abraham from these stones!

lessons.still: If your marriage has ever been through a breach of trust, large or small, you don’t need to rush to revisit the details right now. Simply say quietly to the Lord: “Lord, you know our wounds. Please be our healer.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: After doing wrong, the self-ruled life wants to turn the page fast: “I already apologized—what more do you want?” That is still self on the throne, demanding that the other person heal on my timetable. Self-emptied repentance hands control to God, humbly accepts the process, and slowly proves through actions that life has truly changed.
lessons.jesus: Peter denied the Lord three times. After the resurrection, Jesus neither pretended nothing had happened nor shamed him. Instead he asked him three times, “Do you love me?” and each question rebuilt a little more. Jesus shows us that restoration needs honesty, and it also needs grace and time; he does not give up on those who fail.
lessons.pray: Merciful Lord, you heal the brokenhearted and bind up their wounds. Wherever we have hidden things from each other or hurt each other, lead us to confess honestly and turn away sincerely. Give comfort and protection to the one who was hurt, and humility and perseverance to the one who did wrong. Rebuild the trust between us with your own hands. Amen.
teach: Trust is like a mirror: once it’s shattered, even if you piece it back together, the cracks remain. Breaches of trust in marriage come in all sizes: a hidden purchase, a string of lies, a relationship with someone of the opposite sex that crossed the line. The hurt spouse often says, “I can forgive you, but I don’t know if I can trust you again.” That statement is honest, not unspiritual.

Proverbs says, “He who conceals his sins doesn’t prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy” (Proverbs 28:13). The first step in rebuilding trust is for the one who broke it to confess fully—without downplaying it or shifting blame onto the other—and to truly turn away from it. John the Baptist said, “produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke 3:8). Trust is not restored by one “I’m sorry,” but by consistent actions over a long time: being open without being asked, accepting accountability, and waiting patiently.

We must also say this gently but clearly: forgiveness means laying down our right to revenge before God, and it can be a decision; trust, though, takes time to rebuild and doesn’t have to happen overnight. If the hurt is deep, please seek professional help from a pastor and a marriage counselor. If there is violence, threats, or control, safety comes first—forgiveness does not mean staying in danger. God can heal, and he often heals through the people he sends.
q: Is there anything I am still hiding that I need to confess before God?
When my spouse does wrong, do I demand that they change in my way and at my pace?
talk: Is there something between us where you’d like me to be more open, so you can feel more secure? Please say it gently.
If we’ve ever had a small crack in our trust, what do you think helped it slowly mend? If your spouse can’t join you right now, write down what you’d like to say to them.
acts: Without being asked, tell your spouse about something you’ve seldom explained before
If there is something you need to confess, first write it down before God
For couples who need help, find a trustworthy pastor or counselor ahead of time
lessons.noon: “whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy” — Lord, right now I want to be honest before you and stop hiding.

lessons.title: He Who Calls You Is Faithful
lessons.theme: We may be unfaithful, but he will do it

v: May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely. May your whole spirit, soul, and body be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
He who calls you is faithful, who will also do it.
If we are faithless, he remains faithful; for he can’t deny himself.”

lessons.still: Looking back over this week, you may have seen many places where you weren’t faithful enough. Don’t let condemnation weigh you down. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, I can be unfaithful, but you are still faithful. Today I give our marriage to you.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keeping covenant in our own strength eventually leads either to pride (“I’m more faithful than you”) or to despair (“I can’t do it”). The Holy Spirit is my guide: only as the faithful God works within us can we keep our covenant self-emptied, and give all the glory to him.
lessons.jesus: Before he ascended, Jesus promised, “Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). The disciples had been weak and had run away, but Jesus’ presence was not a reward for their performance; it was his faithful promise. Jesus shows us that faithfulness means not leaving.
lessons.pray: Faithful Father, you called us into marriage, and you will complete your work in us. Even when we are faithless, you remain faithful. Be the anchor of our marriage; catch us when we slip, and keep us faithful to you and to each other all our lives, until the day the Lord Jesus returns. Amen.
teach: In mountain climbing, the other end of the rope is tied to a solid anchor, so the climber dares to keep going up. Even if a foot slips, they won’t fall. Faithfulness in marriage needs an anchor like that. Paul says, “If we are faithless, he remains faithful; for he can’t deny himself” (2 Timothy 2:13). Our faithfulness will slip, but the anchor is God himself.

Paul blesses the believers: “May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely,” and then says, “He who calls you is faithful, who will also do it” (1 Thessalonians 5:23–24). It was God who called us into this marriage, and it is God who takes responsibility for shaping us to be more like Christ. Our part is to cooperate; his promise is to do it. That means we don’t have to grit our teeth and hold on in our own strength.

This week we have seen that faithfulness comes from God, shows itself in doing what we say and being faithful in small things, and includes repair after a breach. Finally, remember that faithfulness is not perfection; it is returning to the covenant even after failure. A faithful couple is not one that never falls, but one that, having fallen, comes back together before the faithful God and says once more, “I do.”
q: This week, where have I most clearly seen my need for God’s faithfulness?
Have past failures made me afraid to make commitments to my spouse again?
talk: Looking back on this week, what fruit of faithfulness have you seen in me?
If we said “I do” to each other again today, what one line would you most like to add?
acts: Tell your spouse once today: “I still do.”
Write down one small commitment you want to keep holding to this week
Memorize Lamentations 3:23 and say it together before bed
lessons.noon: “He who calls you is faithful, who will also do it” — Lord, right now I trust you to complete your work in our home.

mem.t: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

date.t: An Evening with the Volume Turned Down
s: Choose a quiet evening. Turn off the TV and phones, light a small lamp, and make a pot of warm tea.
All evening, deliberately speak a little more softly and slowly than usual, and notice how the atmosphere at home changes.
Take turns finishing this sentence: “The time you treated me with gentleness that I’ll never forget was...”
Read Proverbs 15:1 together, then pray a blessing over each other’s words: “Lord, make our tongues a tree of life.”

lessons.title: Gentleness Is Not Weakness
lessons.theme: Gentleness is strength tamed and governed by God

v: Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Cushite woman whom he had married; for he had married a Cushite woman.
They said, “Has the LORD indeed spoken only with Moses? Hasn’t he spoken also with us?” And the LORD heard it.
Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth.
Blessed are the gentle, for they shall inherit the earth.

lessons.still: Make a tight fist and feel its strength, then slowly open your hand and relax it. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, I have strength, and I have a temper. Today I want to place them in your hands and let you govern them.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Proud strength wants to prove, “I’m right, I’m stronger than you”—it grabs for power and wants to be king. Gentleness hands strength back to God and returns to our rightful place: let people be people, and let God be God. When husband and wife are both willing to be governed by God, home is no longer a wrestling ring.
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was arrested, Peter drew his sword to defend him, but Jesus said, “Or do you think that I couldn’t ask my Father, and he would even now send me more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matthew 26:53). He had unmatched power, yet chose not to use it to protect himself. Jesus’ gentleness was not powerlessness; it was mighty power governed by the Father’s will.
lessons.pray: Lord, you are the Almighty God, yet you treat us gently. Govern our strength, our tempers, and our tongues, so that we don’t use our strength to overpower each other but to serve each other. Make us gentle people, with clear convictions and soft hearts, showing your character in our home. Amen.
teach: A fine horse runs fast and is far stronger than any person, yet once it has been tamed, a light pull on the reins from its rider brings it to a stop. Its strength hasn’t disappeared; it is simply under control. That is exactly what the Bible means by gentleness: not the absence of strength, but strength governed by God. Jesus said, “Blessed are the gentle, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5).

Numbers says, “Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth” (Numbers 12:3). The word translated “humble” here also carries the sense of meekness and gentleness. Moses was no weakling: he dared to face Pharaoh and led Israel out of Egypt. But when his own sister and brother spoke against him, he didn’t rush to hit back; he left the matter with God. That is gentleness: having the power to strike back, and choosing not to use it.

At home, it’s easy to misunderstand gentleness, thinking it means never speaking up, having no opinions, letting others push you around. In fact, gentle people can hold clear convictions and can say “no”; they just don’t use a sharp tone or try to crush the other person. Gentleness is not a quiet voice but a heart governed by God; it isn’t having no boundaries, but still loving within those boundaries.
q: Have I ever mistaken gentleness for weakness, and so been unwilling to be gentle?
At home, has my strength (my way with words, my emotions, my finances, my physical strength) been used to overpower my spouse?
talk: When do you think I’m most gentle? When am I least gentle? Please say it gently.
Is there a topic in our home that often turns into a “wrestling match”? How could we talk about it differently?
acts: Today, before you speak, say in your heart: “Lord, please govern me.”
Identify one situation in which you habitually speak in a forceful tone
Say one gentle word of affirmation to your spouse
lessons.noon: “Blessed are the gentle” — Lord, right now govern my strength and my temper.

lessons.title: A Gentle Answer Turns Away Wrath
lessons.theme: One gentle word can put out a fire

v: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools gush out folly.
The LORD’s eyes are everywhere, keeping watch on the evil and the good.
A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but deceit in it crushes the spirit.

lessons.still: Recall the moment the last argument broke out at home. Which words set the fire going? Don’t blame anyone; just gently ask the Lord: “Lord, next time, let me be the one who pours on water.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Living from the head by ourselves, our first reaction is to justify and hit back, and the more we talk, the more upset we get. Living from the heart by the Spirit, we can pause for a second before we speak and ask, “Lord, am I about to pour water or oil?” Pride provokes pride, but gentleness draws out gentleness.
lessons.jesus: During his trial, an officer struck Jesus. He neither cursed nor shrank back in silence, but calmly said, “If I have spoken evil, testify of the evil; but if well, why do you beat me?” (John 18:23). Jesus shows us that gentleness doesn’t mean not telling the truth; it means speaking calmly and clearly even under provocation.
lessons.pray: Lord, keep us from harsh words and give us gentle answers. When the other is angry, help us pour on water instead of oil; when we want to defend ourselves, help us listen first and pause first. May our tongues be a tree of life in our home, bringing each other healing and rest. Amen.
teach: When a kitchen fire breaks out, some people pour on water and some pour on oil, with completely different results. Proverbs says, “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1). When spouses argue, every reply is really a choice: water or oil? If my spouse is already angry and I answer even louder, I’m pouring oil on the fire.

A gentle answer isn’t lying or pretending everything’s fine; it’s telling the truth in a way the other person can receive. Say your spouse complains, “You forgot again!” A harsh answer is, “Like you never forget anything!” A gentle answer is, “I’m sorry, I really did forget. I know it matters to you. Can I make it up now?” The situation itself hasn’t changed, but the atmosphere is completely different.

Proverbs goes on: “A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but deceit in it crushes the spirit” (Proverbs 15:4). Our tongues can plant a tree of life at home, where others can rest in its shade—or become a knife that crushes the spirit. Our most gentle moments are often not when we’re in a good mood, but when our spouse is upset and we choose to catch them with gentleness.
q: In an argument, what’s the line I most often use to “pour on oil”?
When my spouse is upset, how do I usually respond?
talk: When I speak, which tone hurts you most easily? Which tone makes you feel most “caught” and held?
Let’s come up with one “gentle answer” together that we can open with the next time there’s conflict.
acts: Today, pause for one second before responding to your spouse
Rewrite one sharp thing you often say into a gentle version
In a gentle voice, say thank you to someone in your family
lessons.noon: “A gentle answer turns away wrath” — Lord, right now let me speak words that put out anger.

lessons.title: Learning Gentleness from Jesus
lessons.theme: Take his yoke and learn his gentle and humble ways

v: Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”
He won’t break a bruised reed. He won’t quench a smoking flax, until he leads justice to victory.

lessons.still: Imagine Jesus sitting right beside you. There is no blame in his eyes, only gentleness. Quietly listen as he says to you: “Come to me, and learn from me.” Place today’s weariness and impatience under his gentle gaze.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Jesus is my example. In him, gentleness and humility belong together: those who are humble in heart are gentle with others; those who are proud in heart naturally speak sharply. To bear the fruit of gentleness, our roots must go down into self-emptied humility.
lessons.jesus: When Jesus entered Jerusalem, the people were waiting for a mighty king, yet he fulfilled the words of Scripture: “behold, your King comes to you, humble, and riding on a donkey” (Matthew 21:5). The King of kings chose a donkey, not a warhorse. Jesus shows us that true authority reveals itself through humility and gentleness.
lessons.pray: Gentle and humble Lord Jesus, thank you that you never break a bruised reed or snuff out a smoldering wick. We want to take your yoke and learn from you. Change what is impatient and sharp in us, so that when the other is at their weakest, we lift them up with your gentleness and make our home a place of rest. Amen.
teach: In the Gospels, Jesus rarely describes his own inner life, but once he said, “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29). A yoke is the wooden frame placed on the necks of two oxen pulling a plow together. In those days, an experienced older ox was often yoked with a young one. Jesus invites us to share his yoke, and step by step learn his gentleness.

Gentleness is not an inborn personality trait but a life learned by following Jesus. Some of us are impatient by nature, some of us are blunt talkers; neither is an excuse, and neither is a reason to despair. Like a young ox yoked to an older one, we may lurch around at first, but gradually our steps fall into rhythm. When husband and wife are both under Jesus’ yoke, they become more and more like him, and more and more in step with each other.

Matthew quotes Isaiah to describe Jesus: “He won’t break a bruised reed. He won’t quench a smoking flax” (Matthew 12:20)—a lamp wick that is barely smoldering. When our spouse is weak, weary, or has failed, they are like a bruised reed or a smoldering wick. At that moment, one criticism might snap them, one sigh might snuff them out. Learning Jesus’ gentleness means carefully lifting them up and gently shielding them when they are at their most fragile.
q: Is my spouse like a “bruised reed” in some area right now? How have I been treating them?
What impatience or sharpness have I written off as “just my personality,” unwilling to let Jesus change it?
talk: In what area lately have you felt like a “smoldering wick,” needing me to be especially gentle with you?
Where do you think the two of us are most out of step? How could we keep pace with Jesus together?
acts: Today, choose not to criticize one of your spouse’s weaknesses
Say something protective, such as: “Take your time—it’s okay.”
Write Matthew 11:29 on a sticky note and put it where you’ll see it often
lessons.noon: “I am gentle and humble in heart” — Lord Jesus, right now I want to learn your gentle and humble ways.

lessons.title: Restoring with a Gentle Spirit
lessons.theme: When our spouse falls, gentleness restores rather than condemns

v: Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.
Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
The Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, able to teach, patient,
in gentleness correcting those who oppose him. Perhaps God may give them repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth,

lessons.still: Think of a time when you yourself fell or did something wrong. How did you most want others to treat you? Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, teach me to treat my spouse the way you have gently treated me.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: When the self-ruled life sees a spouse do wrong, what wells up is, “See? I told you so!”—using the other’s failure to lift ourselves up. The self-emptied life sees, “They need help, and I could fall too.” The focus is not on condemning but on restoring; people matter more than issues.
lessons.jesus: When the disciples were weak, Jesus often lifted them up first, then taught them. When Peter began to sink in the water, “Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him, ‘You of little faith, why did you doubt?’” (Matthew 14:31). Jesus took hold of him first, then spoke; his correction always came after his gentle hand.
lessons.pray: Lord, you never look down on our weakness, and you always gently restore us. Forgive us for rushing to condemn and to prove ourselves right when our spouse falls. Give us gentle hearts and wise words, to lift up first and speak second. And protect everyone in our home, so that our home becomes a safe place where things can be mended. Amen.
teach: When a bone is dislocated, a good doctor doesn’t yank it hard, but uses a precise, gentle technique to ease it back into place. Paul says, “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Galatians 6:1). The word “restore” originally meant to mend or put back in place—like a doctor setting a bone, or a fisherman mending a net.

When our spouse does wrong, our most common reaction is to point out the mistake, prove we’re right, and demand an admission. We may be right on every point, but it’s like yanking a dislocated bone: the other person only hurts more and wants to escape. Paul adds a reminder: “looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted” (Galatians 6:1). Gentle people remember that they too could fall.

We need to say this clearly: restoring with gentleness applies to ordinary weaknesses and faults, not to putting up with harm. Physical, verbal, sexual, or financial abuse and control cannot be fixed by gentleness, and enduring them is never what submission requires. In that situation, safety comes first; forgiveness does not mean staying in danger. Please seek help from a pastor and from professionals right away. Gentleness also includes protecting yourself and your family.
q: When my spouse does wrong, is my first reaction more like “a doctor setting a bone” or “a judge passing sentence”?
Have I ever used my spouse’s failure to prove that I’m better?
talk: When you’ve done something wrong, what would you most like me to say or do first?
Think back to a time I stood by you when you were weak. What made you feel treated gently? If your spouse can’t join you right now, write down what you’d like to say to them.
acts: When your spouse makes a small mistake today, say first: “It’s okay—we’ll sort it out together.”
Set aside one thing you want to “correct” in your spouse, and pray for them first
Today, take the initiative to share one of your spouse’s burdens
lessons.noon: “Bear one another’s burdens” — Lord, right now let me lift people up rather than condemn them.

lessons.title: Gentle Wisdom from Above
lessons.theme: A gentle home yields the fruit of righteousness sown in peace

v: Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show by his good conduct that his deeds are done in gentleness of wisdom.
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

lessons.still: Looking back over this week, was there a moment when you chose gentleness and the air at home changed? Quietly thank the Lord: “Lord, thank you for the work you’ve done in me this week. Keep making me gentle.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: From a human point of view, only force gets results and only the loud get heard; from God’s point of view, the gentle inherit the earth and a gentle answer turns away wrath. Change your mindset and your life will change; a changed life changes how we live, and the relationships in our home change with it.
lessons.jesus: When the crowd wanted to stone the woman caught in adultery, Jesus neither went along with them nor excused her sin. He said to her, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more” (John 8:11). Jesus’ gentleness holds both grace and truth; with gentleness, he brings people back to the right path.
lessons.pray: God who gives wisdom, thank you for teaching us about gentleness this week. Give us the wisdom from above, so that we are peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits. May we sow in peace in our home and reap the fruit of righteousness, so that family and friends sense the gentleness of Jesus in our home. Amen.
teach: Take two identical plots of land: one person plants thorns, another plants fruit trees, and a few years later the scenery is completely different. James says, “Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace” (James 3:18). Every word we say at home, every tone of voice, is a seed. Gentleness is a kind of sowing, and its harvest is a peaceful home.

James asks, “Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show by his good conduct that his deeds are done in gentleness of wisdom” (James 3:13). Interestingly, he ties wisdom and gentleness together. Earthly cleverness is often about winning arguments and speaking impressively; but the wisdom from above is “peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits” (James 3:17). In marriage, winning the argument but losing the relationship is not wisdom.

This week we have seen that gentleness is not weakness but strength governed by God; that a gentle answer turns away wrath; that gentleness is learned from Jesus; and that when our spouse falls, gentleness restores rather than condemns. Gentleness takes time to grow, just as a fruit tree doesn’t grow up overnight. But as long as we keep sharing Jesus’ yoke, the climate in our home will gradually change.
q: This week, at what moment did I most clearly experience the power of gentleness?
At home, have I been sowing more “seeds of peace” or “seeds of strife”?
talk: Looking back on this week, what fruit of gentleness have you seen in me?
If our home had a “gentleness pact,” what is the one clause you’d most like to put in it?
acts: Together with your spouse, write one clause for your home’s “gentleness pact”
Today, handle a small bit of friction in a gentle tone
Thank your spouse for one gentle response this week
lessons.noon: “gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits” — Lord, right now give me gentle wisdom from above.

mem.t: Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint.

s: Together, look back through your notes or in-app course records from Week 9 to Week 21, and each circle the one line that moved you most.
Prepare nine small cards, each with one of the nine fruits written on it. Take turns drawing a card and share one specific example of seeing that fruit in your spouse over these past months.
Each of you choose one fruit you most want to ask God to grow in you next season. Write it on the back of the card and give it to your spouse to keep and to pray for you.
Celebrate with a plate of fruit together, and pray as one: “Lord, thank you for bearing fruit in us. May all the glory be yours.”

lessons.title: A City Without Walls
lessons.theme: Self-control is the wall that guards our hearts and our home

v: Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint.
One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty; one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city.

lessons.still: Take a deep breath, then slowly breathe out. Repeat three times. Notice whether there is any irritation or unease in your heart right now. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, be the gatekeeper of my heart, and govern the emotions that rise and fall within me.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Emotions out of control are really self on the throne: my feelings matter most, and everyone else has to fall in line. Self-control gives the throne to Jesus and lets him govern my heart. Out of the heart is the wellspring of life; guard your heart, and you guard your home.
lessons.jesus: When a Samaritan village refused to welcome Jesus, James and John were so angry they wanted to call fire down from heaven. But Jesus “turned and rebuked them” (Luke 9:55), and they went on to another village. When he was rejected, Jesus didn’t let anger take control; he calmly kept walking the road the Father had given him.
lessons.pray: Lord, we confess that we often can’t govern our own hearts, and that our anger and irritation have hurt those closest to us. Be King in our hearts and rebuild our walls. When our emotions surge, help us stop and turn to you, not letting our emotions take the throne, so that our home has peace and protection. Amen.
teach: In ancient times, a city’s walls were its lifeline. Without walls, enemies could come in at any time, wild animals could roam in, and the people couldn’t sleep safely at night. Proverbs says, “Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint” (Proverbs 25:28). A person who can’t control themselves is like a city with collapsed walls: anyone can come in and plunder, and the first to suffer are usually the family who live there.

The Greek word behind the Spirit’s fruit of “self-control” means “having a firm grip on oneself,” like a rider holding the reins. Proverbs also says, “One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty; one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city” (Proverbs 16:32). In the world’s eyes, capturing a city is impressive; in God’s eyes, mastering your own temper is even more so. The greatest battlefield is not out there but within our own hearts.

The wall most often breached in marriage is our emotions. When we’re exhausted, misunderstood, or under pressure, a single remark can send us out of control. Self-control isn’t suppressing our emotions or pretending all is well; it’s not letting our emotions take the throne. We can say, “I’m really angry right now. Give me ten minutes to calm down, and then let’s talk.” That is rebuilding the wall in the middle of an emotional storm.
q: In what situations am I most likely to lose my “walls” and let my emotions burst out?
When I lose control, who gets hurt most often?
talk: When I’m about to explode, how could I express it so that it’s easier for you to receive?
Could we agree on a way to take a “ten-minute calm-down”? For example, a phrase to say, or a place to go to cool off?
acts: Today, when your emotions flare up, take three deep breaths before you respond
Agree with your spouse on a signal phrase for “I need ten minutes to calm down”
Write down the one situation most likely to make you lose control, and hand it to God
lessons.noon: “one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city” — Lord, right now govern my heart, and don’t let my emotions rule.

lessons.title: Guard My Lips
lessons.theme: Self-control in speech is a couple’s most everyday practice

v: Set a watch, LORD, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.
In the multitude of words there is no lack of disobedience, but he who restrains his lips does wisely.

lessons.still: Close your lips gently and stay quiet for one minute, saying nothing. In that quiet, tell the Lord: “Lord, today let every word I say pass before you first.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: When we live from the head by ourselves, our mouths follow our emotions; when we live from the heart by the Spirit, we ask before we speak: “Will this build someone up?” Don’t hurt people to win an argument. People matter more than issues; relationships matter more than saving face.
lessons.jesus: When the chief priests and elders accused Jesus, “he answered nothing” (Matthew 27:12). It wasn’t that he had nothing to say; he knew when there was no need to defend himself. Yet when it was time to teach, comfort, or rebuke, he spoke clearly and powerfully. Jesus’ words were entirely governed by the Father’s will.
