lessons.pray: LORD, set a watch before our mouths; keep the door of our lips. Forgive us for the times we have hurt each other with words, and for the times we have punished each other with silence. Help us say what needs saying gently, and leave with you what shouldn’t be said. May the words of our mouths be acceptable in your sight. Amen.
teach: It’s easy to squeeze toothpaste out of the tube, but impossible to put it back. Words are the same: once spoken, they can’t be taken back. David prayed, “Set a watch, LORD, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips” (Psalm 141:3). Even David, a mighty warrior, knew his mouth needed a guard on duty. The deepest wounds between husband and wife are seldom made by swords; most are made by words that can’t be unsaid.

Proverbs says, “In the multitude of words there is no lack of disobedience, but he who restrains his lips does wisely” (Proverbs 10:19). In an argument we often think the more we say, the better we prove our point, but usually the more we say, the further off topic we drift and the more we hurt. Self-control in speech isn’t only avoiding foul language; it also means not digging up the past, not mocking, not running down our spouse in front of others, and not jumping to conclusions in anger.

Self-control in speech doesn’t mean the silent treatment or refusing to talk, either. The silent treatment uses silence to punish the other person, and that too is a loss of control. Self-control means saying what needs to be said at the right time and in the right way, and handing to God what shouldn’t be said, rather than saying it. Sometimes the most self-controlled sentence is: “I need to think about this. Let’s talk properly a bit later.”
q: What is something I said recently that I badly wanted to take back afterward?
Am I more prone to a “multitude of words,” or to using the silent treatment to show I’m unhappy?
talk: Of the things I’ve said, which hurt you most and still stays with you? I’m willing to listen, and willing to apologize.
Of the things I’ve said, which made you feel the warmest?
acts: Today, before you speak, ask: Will this build someone up?
Sincerely apologize for something you once said that hurt your spouse
Go the whole day without digging up the past or mocking, and keep watch over your mouth
lessons.noon: “Set a watch, LORD, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.” — Lord, right now please stand guard over my mouth.

lessons.title: Not Brought Under the Power of Anything
lessons.theme: Self-control over our appetites, so phones and spending no longer run the home

v: “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are expedient. “All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be brought under the power of anything.
Every man who strives in the games exercises self-control in all things. Now they do it to receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible.
I therefore run like that, not aimlessly. I fight like that, not beating the air,
but I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be disqualified.

lessons.still: After reading this, place your phone face down for two minutes and be still. Notice whether your hand is itching to pick it up. Gently tell the Lord: “Lord, show me what is quietly becoming my master.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Whatever holds power over us is ruling as king. The right order of relationships is God, self, people, things. When “things” like phones and shopping get ahead of our spouse, the order is turned upside down. Self-control is letting Jesus reign again and putting the order of our home right.
lessons.jesus: After fasting forty days, Jesus was hungry, and the devil told him to turn stones into bread. Jesus answered, “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth” (Matthew 4:4). He had the power to satisfy himself, yet he didn’t let his stomach be master. Jesus shows us that the strength for self-control comes from being fed by God’s word.
lessons.pray: Lord, you are the only Master of our home. Whatever is quietly holding power over us—phones, shopping, work, or any appetite—shine your light on it and set us free. Help us, like athletes, to have a clear goal and self-control, keeping our time and energy for you and for each other, as we run the heavenly race together. Amen.
teach: A fish isn’t caught because the hook is big, but because the bait is so tempting. Paul says, “‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things are expedient. ‘All things are lawful for me,’ but I will not be brought under the power of anything” (1 Corinthians 6:12). Phones, online shopping, good food, binge-watching, even work—none of these are bad in themselves. But when we can’t put them down, they turn from tools into masters.

Paul uses the picture of an athlete: “Every man who strives in the games exercises self-control in all things” (1 Corinthians 9:25). For the sake of the competition, an athlete keeps a disciplined diet, sleep schedule, and use of time—not because those pleasures are sinful, but because he has a more important goal. A couple’s goal is to build a household that belongs to God, so we are willing to exercise self-control even in things that are “lawful,” in order to gain something more precious.

In many homes, intimacy is stolen bit by bit: each scrolling their own phone at dinner, each watching their own shows before bed, weekends filled up with impulse spending and overtime. Self-control isn’t harsh self-denial; it’s clearing space for God and for each other. A couple can agree together on a few simple rules: no phones at the table, talk before any big purchase, and keep some time each evening for each other.
q: What in my life am I unable to “put down”? Has it begun to hold power over me?
How does the time I spend on my phone each day compare with the time I spend with my spouse?
talk: What do you think most easily steals our time with each other at home?
What one simple family rule (like no phones at the table) could we agree on and try starting this week?
acts: At dinner tonight, both of you put your phones in another room
For your next non-essential purchase, wait one day before deciding
Use the half hour you save to take a walk or talk with your spouse
lessons.noon: “I will not be brought under the power of anything” — Lord, right now I put down what is in my hands and let you reign.

lessons.title: Walking by the Spirit
lessons.theme: Self-control comes not from willpower but from the Spirit and grace

v: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.
For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary to one another, that you may not do the things that you desire.
For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men,
instructing us to the intent that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we would live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present age;

lessons.still: Maybe you have resolved to change before, only to fail again and again. Don’t lose heart. Quietly tell the Lord: “Holy Spirit, I admit I can’t do this on my own. Today I hand you the steering wheel. Please guide me.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Holy Spirit is my guide. When we try to control ourselves in our own strength, success easily makes us proud and failure easily makes us beat ourselves up; either way, the focus is still on self. When we walk by the Spirit, the focus is on Jesus: success is grace, and failure can return to grace and start again. This is self-emptied self-control.
lessons.jesus: In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus was so sorrowful he felt close to death, yet he prayed, “Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). This is the deepest self-control: not suppressing feelings, but placing his own will in the Father’s hands. Through prayer, Jesus made it through the hardest night of all.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, we confess that in our own strength we cannot overcome the desires of the flesh. Fill us and guide our steps, so that we walk by you. Thank you that your grace not only forgives us but also teaches us every day. Make us spiritual companions to each other, supporting and praying for one another on the road of self-control. Amen.
teach: Picture one person rowing hard against the current, wearing themselves out, yet still being swept back to where they started; and another person raising a sail and gliding forward with the wind. Many couples’ experience of self-control is like the first: many resolutions, and in the end, failure. But Paul says, “walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh” (Galatians 5:16). Self-control is the fruit of the Spirit, not the result of gritting our teeth.

Paul is very honest: “For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh” (Galatians 5:17). There really is a tug-of-war going on inside us. That’s not strange, and it’s no reason to despair. The key isn’t fighting the flesh harder but yielding more to the Spirit: drawing near to God first thing in the morning, praying immediately when temptation comes, and letting each other be spiritual companions who remind and pray for one another.

Titus says God’s grace is “instructing us to the intent that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we would live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present age” (Titus 2:12). To live “soberly” is to live a clear-headed, self-controlled life. So grace doesn’t only forgive us; like a coach, it trains us day by day in a new way of living. We don’t practice self-control in order to be saved; we learn self-control because we have already received grace.
q: In what area have I been “rowing” by willpower alone, and failing repeatedly?
When temptation comes, do I turn first to the Holy Spirit or to my own methods?
talk: Is there an area where you want to grow in self-control and would like me to support you in prayer?
How can we be spiritual companions to each other, helping with gentle reminders rather than accusations?
acts: When temptation comes, immediately pray a short prayer: “Holy Spirit, help me.”
Tell your spouse one area where you want to practice self-control, and ask them to pray for you
Before bed, pray for each other for one minute
lessons.noon: “walk by the Spirit” — Holy Spirit, right now I hand you the steering wheel.

lessons.title: Remain in the Lord, Bear Much Fruit
lessons.theme: Looking back on thirteen weeks: the fruit God has borne in us

v: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer.
Every branch in me that doesn’t bear fruit, he takes away. Every branch that bears fruit, he prunes, that it may bear more fruit.
You are already pruned clean because of the word which I have spoken to you.
Remain in me, and I in you. As the branch can’t bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me.
I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.
being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.

lessons.still: Think back from Week 9 to today. Over these three-plus months, what ups and downs has your home been through? Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, thank you for working in us all along, even when we couldn’t see it.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: This stage of “Life” is exactly 321’s “life first, then relationships, then ministry.” The practice of 920 is this: toward my “2,” live out the self-emptied “0,” and bear the ninefold fruit, the “9.” The fruit is not for boasting about ourselves but for the Father’s glory, so that we let Jesus receive all the glory.
lessons.jesus: Jesus told his disciples, “You didn’t choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John 15:16). Bearing fruit was not a plan the disciples came up with; it was Jesus’ choosing and commissioning. He chose us, and he will see to it that our fruit remains.
lessons.pray: Lord of the vine, thank you for walking with us, pruning us, and watering us all through these thirteen weeks. Thank you for every fruit you have grown in us; large or small, each one is your grace. Help us remain in you, so that our fruit will remain and grow more abundant. May our home bring glory to the Father, and let Jesus receive all the glory. Amen.
teach: A fruit tree doesn’t bear fruit overnight. From blossom to ripe fruit, it takes sunshine and rain, and pruning too. Jesus said, “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit” (John 15:5). These thirteen weeks, we haven’t been learning how to try harder, but how to remain in the Lord.

Look back over the road we’ve traveled. In Weeks 9 to 12, we set out from “We love him, because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19), learning that love is patient, doesn’t seek its own way, and never fails. In Weeks 13 to 21, treating our spouse as our most important “2,” we practiced the nine fruits one by one: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. They are not nine separate fruits, but one fruit borne by the one Spirit.

Perhaps you feel some of the fruit is still small and unripe. Don’t lose heart. Jesus said that every branch that bears fruit, the Father “prunes, that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:2). Paul also says, “he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). Today, please don’t just look at what your spouse still lacks; count together what God has already grown in them.
q: Over these thirteen weeks, in which fruit have I most clearly seen God change me?
Which fruit do I most want to keep asking God to grow in the next stage?
talk: Over these three-plus months, what fruit have you seen God grow in me? Please give one specific example. If your spouse can’t join you right now, write down the fruit you’ve seen in them.
Looking back over Weeks 9 to 21, which week’s content changed our home the most? Why?
acts: Write a card naming one fruit you’ve seen in your spouse
Choose one fruit you want to grow more in the next stage, and tell your spouse
Together, offer God a prayer of thanks for the changes of these thirteen weeks
lessons.noon: “He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit” — Lord, right now I want to remain in you and let you bear fruit.
